grey.question: The film's identity and subject are clear: Pablo Moreno's 2017 Spanish feature about Sister Hélène Studler, the Daughter of Charity whose network in occupied Metz smuggled some two thousand prisoners to safety. It was commissioned by the Vincentian Family, and the director says they wanted a figure close to people of today rather than a saint's life. The one secular review found praises Assumpta Serna but says little about how religious life is shown. A fuller review, or a check of the dialogue, showing that her vocation and prayer stay at the centre would settle it.

summary: Assumpta Serna plays Sister Hélène Studler, a Daughter of Charity in occupied Metz whose escape network smuggled some two thousand prisoners of war to safety.
synopsis: Metz, 1940. Sister Hélène Studler, a Daughter of Charity who cares for orphans and the destitute at a city hospice, sees Lorraine annexed and a camp for French prisoners of war built near the city. Under Red Cross protection she and her sisters, with volunteers from the town, bring the prisoners food and water. Relief turns into rescue. The sisters begin smuggling men out of the camp and across the new frontier into unoccupied France, and a clandestine network, linked to the Resistance, grows around them. The work puts her community and her helpers in danger. Among those the network helps, in the film as in history, are the future president François Mitterrand and General Henri Giraud. St Louise de Marillac, co-foundress of her congregation, appears as a figure in the story.
inclusion: Hélène Studler's story is little known outside Lorraine, and no French film has told it. Moreno made this one on a budget of roughly half a million euros, commissioned by the Vincentian Family for the 400th anniversary of its charism, with Burgos standing in for Lorraine and Spanish actors playing French and Germans. Miguel Ángel Pizarro of eCartelera, the only secular critic found, called Assumpta Serna's performance one of her strongest in years and said she carries the film over its weak early production design, which he compared unfavourably with Spanish television drama. He found the faith shown as the heroine's inner strength rather than as propaganda. The press average on SensaCine is low. It is a modest, sincere film whose main interest is the true story and Serna.
themes: Sister Hélène acts as a Daughter of Charity: the film roots her rescue work in the Vincentian tradition of serving the poor, Catholic accounts describe her as sustained by prayer, and St Louise de Marillac appears. The director calls his approach Christian humanism and says the Vincentians wanted a figure close to people of today rather than a saint's biography; the anniversary campaign the film served took the text 'I was a stranger and you welcomed me'. Pizarro reads the faith as her inner strength. How much the film shows of her religious life, prayer, community and obedience, as against the humanitarian adventure, no independent review says.
history: Marie Joséphine Studler (1891–1944), born at Amiens to an Alsatian family, joined the Daughters of Charity in 1912 and worked at the Saint-Nicolas hospice in Metz from 1918. From 1940 to early 1942 she ran an escape network for prisoners of war, draft evaders and Allied airmen, credited with helping over 2,000 people. She was arrested in 1941 and released for ill health. Her network helped Mitterrand escape in December 1941, and from Lyon she found the guide for Giraud's escape in 1942. She died of cancer at Clermont-Ferrand on 3 December 1944.

title: Quo Vadis
decision: PUBLISH: Re-checked against the AFI Catalog's full synopsis. The joint suicide is real but belongs to the pagan Petronius and his slave Eunice, while the Christians die by martyrdom and Nero's own suicide is shown as cowardice; the coercive start of the romance is Nero's act, which Lygia escapes and refuses until Vinicius turns towards Christ. Neither is endorsed by the film. Liz Gloyn and the Dickinson College essay give substantive treatment. Both elements are flagged in advisories.
summary: MGM's Technicolor epic of Nero's Rome sets a Roman commander's pursuit of a Christian girl against the Great Fire, the first persecution and the deaths of St Peter and St Paul.
synopsis: In AD 64 the commander Marcus Vinicius returns to Rome and falls for Lygia, a Christian hostage raised by a retired general. When she rebuffs him, his uncle Petronius gets Nero to hand her to Marcus as a gift; her giant servant Ursus rescues her. Marcus tracks her to a secret gathering where St Peter tells of his time with Christ. Lygia will not marry him at the price of her faith. Nero burns Rome to inspire a poem and, to save himself, blames the Christians. On the Appian Way Peter meets his Lord and turns back to Rome. Christians are thrown to the lions, Peter is crucified, Petronius takes his own life, and Lygia is tied in the arena before a bull, with Ursus her only defender.
inclusion: This is the film that started the 1950s epic cycle, and it has the virtues and faults of the type. The sets, crowds and Robert Surtees's colour photography are lavish; the burning of Rome is spectacular. Peter Ustinov's Nero, vain, petulant and murderous, steals the picture, and Leo Genn's ironic Petronius runs him close. Robert Taylor and Deborah Kerr are stiff, and the romance is the weakest part. What surprises modern viewers, as the classicist Liz Gloyn found, is how central the Church is: Peter and Paul appear in person, the catacomb liturgy and Peter's preaching are given time, and the martyrs go to the lions singing. The Christian community is idealised but attractive.
themes: The film's subject is the Church's first persecution and the witness of the martyrs. Peter recounts the miraculous catch and the Resurrection, the Domine, quo vadis legend sends him back to Rome to die, and he is crucified head downward, as tradition reports. Paul preaches that Christ conquers by love. Lygia prays for Marcus's conversion and refuses to buy his love with her faith; Peter marries them in prison. Against this the film sets Roman decadence and Nero's claim to divinity. Petronius dies as a cultivated pagan; the contrast with the Christians who 'know how to die' is the point.
history: Rome burned in July 64, and Nero blamed the Christians, whom Tacitus records were killed in his gardens. Early tradition, reported by Origen through Eusebius, says Peter was crucified head downward at his own wish; the date of his death is uncertain within 64 to 68. The Quo vadis encounter on the Appian Way is an ancient legend, not a scriptural event. Petronius's forced suicide is recorded by Tacitus.
liberties: Lygia, Vinicius and Ursus are fictional, from Henryk Sienkiewicz's 1896 novel. The joint suicide with a slave is borrowed from Seneca and Paulina, who survived. There is no evidence that Poppaea proposed blaming the Christians. Nero's death and Galba's arrival are compressed into the aftermath of the persecution. The flowering staff is a pious legend.
advisories:
A long scene shows Petronius and his slave Eunice opening their veins and dying at table; it is calm and bloodless but sympathetic to them.

Christians are killed by lions and burned at the stake, mostly offscreen; Nero strangles Poppaea and is helped to stab himself; sword fights and a man's neck broken.

Nero orders Lygia given to Marcus as a slave at the start; scantily dressed dancers and Roman revels.

Younger children may find the arena scenes frightening.

title: Fabiola
decision: GREY: The reservation is documented by contemporary pre-conciliar Catholic evidence: Paola Palma's archival study (Schermi, 2017) shows the Centro Cattolico Cinematografico classified the Italian release 'adulti con riserva', and Vittorino Veronese of Catholic Action found it 'molto discutibile' for its thesis and sensual material. The English subtitle file shows what that thesis is: not indifferentism, since the Christians say Rome must become Christian and the martyrs confess Christ, but non-violence and human brotherhood. The film is dedicated to the victims of all violence, its Christians speak of a world without masters or slaves, and Rhual's refusal to kill rests on the claim that a Christian never kills. No baptism occurs. Not REJECT; the rating and the sensual material keep it GREY.

grey.question: Fabiola was sold as a Catholic epic, but the Italian Catholic film office of its day classified it 'adults with reservations', and Catholic Action's Vittorino Veronese found its thesis questionable and its sensual scenes gratuitous. The dialogue shows a thesis of non-violence and human brotherhood, dedicated to the victims of all violence, with an absolute refusal to kill that goes beyond Catholic teaching on just defence. Yet the martyrs confess Christ plainly, and Fabiola declares herself a Christian in the arena. The question is whether that witness outweighs a gladiator romance, the sensual scenes and the loose use of Wiseman's novel.

summary: Blasetti's huge postwar epic, very loosely from Cardinal Wiseman's novel, turns the Church of the catacombs into a gladiator romance and murder plot that ends in the arena.
synopsis: In Rome around 312, Fabiola, a senator's daughter, falls for Rhual, a Gaulish gladiator who is secretly an agent of Constantine. Her father, Senator Fabius, who favours tolerance and the freeing of slaves, is murdered, and the Christians are blamed and put on trial. Rhual is condemned with them to the arena. Fabiola at first suspects him, then takes her stand with the Christians in the arena. Rhual refuses to kill his opponents and the other gladiators follow him. Constantine's army reaches Rome, the city rises, and the film ends under the Christian standards of the new emperor.
inclusion: Fabiola opened the postwar wave of religious epics, as the Treccani film encyclopedia notes, and it was the biggest Italian spectacle since the war: Michèle Morgan, Henri Vidal and Michel Simon, enormous sets, and the top box office of its Italian season. French critics in 1949, as Paola Palma's archival study shows, admired Blasetti's handling of crowds while finding the film too long. Time Out's reviewer finds it dull until the violent climax in the arena; Manny Farber, seeing the shortened American version, called it a chaos of disconnected sequences. Its interest now is largely historical: an ambitious Catholic spectacle in postwar Italy, made by a company widely taken for a Vatican enterprise, whose Catholic credentials the Catholic film bodies then publicly disowned.
themes: Wiseman's 1854 novel is a Catholic apologetic for the Church of the catacombs, ending in Fabiola's baptism. The film keeps the persecution, the arena and names such as Sebastiano, Cecilia and Sira, but builds its story on an invented gladiator who serves Constantine, a murder mystery and a love affair. A French critic in 1949 complained that Fabiola reaches Christianity by way of profane passion, and Veronese judged the thesis questionable. The dialogue shows what he meant: the film is dedicated to the victims of all violence, and its Christians preach brotherhood, a world without masters or slaves and an absolute refusal to kill, which goes beyond the Church's teaching on just defence. Yet the faith is not diluted: the martyrs confess Christ, and Fabiola declares herself a Christian in the arena.
history: Salvo D'Angelo's Universalia Film made Fabiola with French money and stars through Franco-London Films, though it was not an official co-production. It opened in Italy on 3 March 1949 and in France a few months later. The Centro Cattolico Cinematografico classified the Italian commercial version 'adults with reservations'. The Dominican Félix Morlion had praised it in the OCIC's new review, expecting cuts he had asked for; they were never made, and a correction in his name accepted the Catholic office's rating. Shortened dubbed versions reached Britain and America in 1951. A restoration was presented in Rome in 2001.
liberties: Rhual, the gladiator-agent of Constantine, the murder of Fabiola's father and the love story are invented. The novel's martyrdoms of Agnes, Pancratius and Tarcisius do not appear in the cast lists consulted. The film sets its action around 312, on the eve of Constantine's victory, rather than in the Diocletian persecution where Wiseman places most of the story, and it ends with Constantine's army entering Rome. The baptism of Fabiola and her household that the novel narrates does not occur in the dialogue.
advisories:
Prolonged kisses and love scenes, a banquet dance and semi-nude courtesans: the material a 1949 Catholic critic asked to have cut.

Arena martyrdoms and mass violence at the climax.

Classified 'adults with reservations' by the Italian Catholic film office in 1949. Adults and older teenagers.

Versions vary widely, from the Italian release of about 164 minutes to an American dubbed cut of about 97, and the French release differed again. Check which version a copy is.

title: Diary of a Country Priest
alternateTitles: Le Journal d'un curé de campagne
decision: PUBLISH: Steven Greydanus's detailed review and the critical tradition around the film establish a portrait of priestly perseverance and grace in apparent failure, drawn faithfully from Bernanos. Adult material (an affair, a threatened suicide) is part of the moral drama and is disclosed.
summary: Bresson's spare adaptation of Bernanos follows a sickly young curé whose parish rejects him, and finds holiness in apparent failure.
synopsis: A young priest arrives in Ambricourt, a village in northern France. He is poor, ill, inexperienced and awkward, and his parishioners respond with indifference or mockery. He records everything in a diary. The older curé of Torcy gives him blunt advice about running a parish. At the château, the count is having an affair with the governess, and the count's daughter Chantal hates them both and threatens to kill herself. The priest confronts the countess, who has been bitter towards God since the death of her son. In a long exchange she yields and makes her peace, and she dies that night. Gossip about the encounter turns the village further against him. Diagnosed with stomach cancer, he travels to Lille and dies in the lodgings of a former seminary friend who has left the priesthood.
inclusion: This is one of the essential films about the priesthood. Bresson strips away everything decorative: Claude Laydu's still face, the diary voice-over, Léonce-Henry Burel's grey images of the Artois countryside. What remains is a man trying to do his duty with almost no visible success. The scene with the countess is the dramatic peak; Greydanus compares it to the great dialogues in The Brothers Karamazov. André Bazin's 1951 essay on the film helped make it a landmark of modern cinema. It won the Prix Louis Delluc and the International Award and OCIC (Catholic) prize at Venice. The pace is slow and the tone severe, and some viewers find it opaque. It rewards patience.
themes: The film's subject is the priesthood stripped of consolation. The curé suffers spiritual dryness, physical weakness and the contempt of his flock. He feels unable even to pray, yet keeps saying Mass, visiting and hearing confessions. Greydanus notes how he accepts failure, dryness and persecution and turns them into a kind of victory. The countess scene shows the cure of souls in action: he refuses to accept her despair and leads her to surrender her grief to God. The end gives Bernanos's last words to the priest: "All is grace." The film treats a priest's life as fruitful in ways he cannot see.
history: Georges Bernanos published his novel Journal d'un curé de campagne in 1936; it won the Grand Prix du roman of the Académie française. Bernanos died in 1948, before Bresson's adaptation. The curé is fictional, though Bernanos drew on the rural clergy of the Pas-de-Calais.
liberties: Bresson follows the novel closely but cuts heavily, especially the long reflective passages and several conversations with the curé of Torcy. He invents almost nothing; his changes are mainly omissions and a sharper focus on the priest's isolation.
advisories:
An adulterous affair (implied, not shown).

A girl threatens suicide; a death; terminal illness.

Slow and austere; best for older teenagers and adults.

title: I Confess
decision: PUBLISH: America's Catholic Movie Club essay, TCM and the AFI Catalog establish the seal of confession as the film's governing moral fact; the priest keeps it at the risk of his life. Mature material (murder, blackmail, a past romance) is disclosed.
summary: Hitchcock's most Catholic film: a Quebec priest hears a murderer's confession and then, bound by the seal, cannot clear himself when suspicion falls on him.
synopsis: In Quebec City, Otto Keller, a German refugee who works at the parish, confesses to Father Michael Logan that he has killed a lawyer named Villette during a robbery, wearing a cassock as a disguise. Witnesses saw a priest leaving the house. Inspector Larrue learns that Villette had been blackmailing Ruth Grandfort, a married woman who had loved Logan before his ordination, and Logan becomes the chief suspect. He will not say what he knows. Keller, increasingly afraid, plants evidence against him. Logan is tried, acquitted for want of proof and jeered by a hostile crowd outside the courthouse, before the truth comes out in a confrontation at the Château Frontenac.
inclusion: Hitchcock, raised a Catholic and taught by Jesuits, built a thriller around a rule most of his audience did not understand, and the film's power comes from treating that rule as absolute. Montgomery Clift plays Logan almost entirely through silence and posture. Robert Burks's location photography makes Quebec's steep streets and churches part of the drama. The flaws are real: Hitchcock himself thought it heavy-handed and humourless, and the Ruth flashbacks are stiff. But few Hollywood films show a priest paying so high a price for keeping the seal, and none does it with more conviction.
themes: The seal of confession is the hinge of the plot. Logan may not reveal what Keller told him, even to save himself from the gallows, and he never considers doing so. Hitchcock blamed the film's weak box office on audiences who did not grasp why a priest would stay silent. John Dougherty, writing in America, calls it a uniquely Catholic moral conundrum. The film also draws the contrast between the penitent's duty and the priest's: Keller confesses but does not make amends, and his fear drives him to frame the man bound to protect his secret.
history: The screenplay by George Tabori and William Archibald adapts Paul Anthelme's 1902 French play Nos deux consciences. Hitchcock had owned the rights for years. Warner Bros. vetoed the original ending, in which the priest is executed before his innocence is proved, and a pre-ordination illegitimate child, according to TCM "for fear of offending Catholics". The film was shot on location in Quebec City, with a priest, Father Paul LaCouline, credited as technical adviser.
liberties: This is fiction, not a reconstructed case. The investigation and trial are simplified for suspense. The play's darker ending, in which the innocent priest dies, was replaced at the studio's insistence, and the play's illegitimate child was cut.
advisories:
A murder, blackmail and a police shooting.

Flashbacks to the priest's pre-ordination romance with a woman who had married another man; restrained.

Suitable for teenagers and adults.

title: Angels of Sin
decision: PUBLISH: Doug Cummings's detailed essay and the BFI record establish a drama of zeal, pride, humility and repentance inside a Dominican congregation that receives women from prison; the ending joins the religious and the legal acceptance of guilt. Murder and emotional cruelty are disclosed.
summary: Bresson's first feature: a novice in a convent for former prisoners sets out to save a hardened young woman, and has to be saved from her own pride first.
synopsis: Anne-Marie, a well-off young woman with a fervent vocation, enters the Dominican Sisters of Bethany, a congregation that welcomes women released from prison. Accompanying the sisters to collect a released inmate, she fixes on another prisoner, Thérèse, who insists she was framed by her former lover. On release, Thérèse shoots him, then takes refuge in the convent as a novice. Anne-Marie's possessive zeal to convert her irritates the community and leads to her own humiliation and expulsion. She keeps vigil by the grave of the congregation's founder and falls gravely ill. Readmitted and dying, she is nursed by Thérèse, who is finally moved by her. As Anne-Marie dies, the police arrive, and Thérèse holds out her wrists.
inclusion: Made under the Occupation by a director just back from a German prison camp, this is a remarkable debut. The style is not yet the bare Bresson of later films. There are professional actresses, a score and Jean Giraudoux's polished dialogue. But the concentration is already there in the white habits, the closed spaces and the faces of Renée Faure and Jany Holt. Doug Cummings shows how carefully the film weighs Anne-Marie's humility against her pride, and the convent's rivalries against its charity. It is not a sentimental convent picture. The community is petty at times, and the heroine is often wrong. That honesty makes the final act of grace convincing.
themes: The film is about the purification of zeal. Anne-Marie genuinely wants to save a soul, but her charity becomes possessive and proud, and the community's discipline, including penance and obedience, exposes this. Her suffering and death become the means of Thérèse's conversion. The film insists that repentance includes accepting earthly justice: Thérèse's surrender to the police completes her change of heart rather than contradicting it. The religious community is shown with its faults, but its vocation and rule are taken seriously.
history: The Dominican Sisters of Bethany were founded in 1866 by the Dominican Jean-Joseph Lataste, who had preached in women's prisons and wanted a community in which former prisoners and women without a criminal past lived as equals. The Dominican priest Raymond-Léopold Bruckberger proposed a film about them and worked on the script with Bresson and Jean Giraudoux. Producer Roland Tual took over the project after Pathé dropped it. It was released in 1943.
liberties: Anne-Marie, Thérèse and the crime are fictional. The congregation is real, but the film condenses its life into a few dramatic months, sharpens its internal rivalries, and gives Giraudoux's literary dialogue to its sisters. It is not a documentary of Bethany houses.
advisories:
A deliberate killing (shown in preparation, act brief).

Humiliation, emotional cruelty, illness and death.

Mature teenagers and adults.

title: I Was a Parish Priest
decision: PUBLISH: the Italian Catholic Cinematografo record gives a full narrative and a 1955 Segnalazioni cinematografiche notice; together they establish a priest who sides with exploited miners and is then sent back to them by his bishop. The 2019 diocesan capsule is retained only for production context; its synopsis echoes the DVD blurb and is not independent criticism.
summary: Rafael Gil's prize-winning drama of a young priest who takes the miners' side in a bitter strike and pays for it with his superiors and his own body.
synopsis: In 1930, Father Andrés Mendoza, just out of the seminary, is sent to Aldemoz, a poor mining village full of resentment. The mine owner, Don César, tries to win him over, while the miners, led by the embittered Martín, distrust him. When a worker is unjustly dismissed, the men strike and occupy the mine. Andrés tries to mediate, fails, and then openly backs the strikers. Don César has to give way but complains to the bishop. Later, the owner's son and Martín's small daughter wander into an abandoned, unstable gallery and have to be rescued. Then a cave-in traps several men, among them Martín, Don César and the priest, until their comrades dig them out. Martín will not reconcile with Don César even underground, but does so at his injured daughter's bedside. The bishop summons Andrés and lets him return to his miners.
inclusion: This is one of the more interesting Spanish religious films of the 1950s because it takes sides. Rafael Gil and the writers Vicente Escrivá and Ramón D. Faraldo give the young priest a real fight, on the side of the workers, against the man who owns the mine. Claude Laydu, two years after Diary of a Country Priest, plays another young curé, dubbed into Spanish. Francisco Rabal won best-actor prizes as Martín. The 1955 Italian Catholic notice found the opening slow and somewhat naive but called the mine sequence intense and convincing and praised the photography. It won the top prize at the first San Sebastián festival and was also shown at Venice.
themes: The film puts the Church's social teaching into the mouth of a parish priest. Andrés defends a just wage and fair treatment, which he sees as part of caring for souls, and he refuses to be the owner's chaplain. The script also checks him. His siding with the strike costs him the trust of his superiors, and the decisive reconciliation comes through suffering and charity in the mine rather than through victory. The bishop's decision to send him back makes the point that the priest's place is with his poor parishioners, under obedience. The approach fits Rerum novarum and Quadragesimo anno rather than any revolutionary programme.
history: Released on 30 September 1953, the film was declared "of national interest" by the Franco regime's film authorities, which brought official support. The Colegio de Médicos reportedly objected to its portrayal of a doctor and sought to have it banned. It won the Gran Premio at the first San Sebastián International Film Festival in 1953. Music is by Joaquín Rodrigo.
liberties: Aldemoz and its strike are fictional. The film should not be taken as a portrait of Spanish labour relations in 1930. The concentration of rescue and reconciliation into a few days is dramatic shorthand.
advisories:
Mining accidents, trapped men and children in danger; a child is injured.

Class hostility and threats.

Best for older children with an adult, teenagers and adults.

title: Balarrasa
decision: PUBLISH: Independent treatment is now substantial: DeCine21's review, Rubén Higueras Flores's close textual analysis (ZER, 2017), Matt Losada's article (Romance Notes, 2011) and Fernán Gómez's own recollection (via Joan Ripollès, Centro Virtual Cervantes). Higueras finds undercurrents linking religion with coercion and renunciation, but concludes they do not overturn the plain reading: a sinner's conversion, a priestly vocation and the restoration of a family to the faith. That reading is sound, and the adult material serves it. Year 1951 (Cannes competition 1951; scholars date the production 1950).
summary: Nieves Conde's postwar melodrama about a reckless Legion officer whose comrade dies in his place, and who becomes a priest and sets out to save his own family.
synopsis: A Spanish missionary is lost in an Alaskan blizzard, and as he faces death he remembers his life. During the Civil War, Lieutenant Javier Mendoza, known as Balarrasa, is a hard-drinking Legion officer. He gambles away his guard duty to a comrade, Joaquín, who is shot on the watch that should have been Javier's. Shaken, he leaves the army for the seminary in Salamanca. Back home as a seminarian, he finds his family in moral ruin: his widowed father gambles, his brother Fernando trades in black-market currency, his sister Lina is the mistress of the crook their father owes money to, and his youngest sister Mayte drifts between suitors. Javier sets about putting them right. Lina dies in a car crash while fleeing with her lover, and the shock brings the family back to the faith. Javier is ordained and leaves for the missions.
inclusion: Balarrasa was one of the most successful Spanish religious films of its time. It was chosen for the Cannes competition in 1951, and it made Fernando Fernán Gómez a leading man; he and Nieves Conde won the Spanish film writers' medals for actor and director. Vicente Escrivá's script is a moral fable, but Nieves Conde gives it a hard edge. The family scenes have the shadows and night-time look of film noir, and the picture of a prosperous postwar family rotting from within anticipates his social drama Surcos. DeCine21 praises the realism, the humour that leavens the drama and Fernán Gómez's performance, and notes that priests advised the production. Fernán Gómez himself later found the family's sins mild stand-ins for the real problems of the time.
themes: This is a vocation story built on guilt and reparation. Javier reads his comrade's death as a debt: the life left to him is not his own, so he gives it to God. The film shows seminary study, Latin and Thomist philosophy, ordination with the kissing of the new priest's hands, and the missions. At home his work is the cure of souls: grace at table, a Gospel warning about empty hands, steady pressure on each sinner. Lina's death, with her empty hands raised and Javier, not yet a priest, unable to absolve her, is a stark lesson about dying unprepared. Higueras Flores argues that the film quietly ties religion to renunciation and coercion, but he concludes that this does not overturn its plain religious meaning.
history: Balarrasa is fiction. Its writer, Vicente Escrivá, co-founded the production company Aspa Films with the director Rafael Gil in 1950 and became a leading maker of Catholic films in 1950s Spain. The story of a Legion officer who exchanges his uniform for a cassock reflects the early Franco years, when the regime increasingly presented itself through the Church rather than the army; Matt Losada and Higueras Flores both read the film in that light.
advisories:
A soldier is shot dead; a fatal car crash; a young woman's deathbed.

title: The Fugitive
decision: PUBLISH: AFI and TCM establish the film and its changes to Greene; Greydanus (A-, +3) and the 1948 Venice International Award (reported as the first OCIC prize) support a reverent treatment of a hunted priest who baptises, seeks to say Mass and dies rather than apostatise. The reservation about the altered protagonist dissolves: the changes remove the novel's sacrilegious and sexual sins rather than add doctrinal error, at the cost of Greene's complexity. Legion of Decency rating not found; verify.
summary: John Ford's stark, stylised version of Greene's The Power and the Glory: Henry Fonda's hunted priest, the last in a state where religion is outlawed, walks back towards martyrdom.
synopsis: In an unnamed Latin American state the government has outlawed religion and hunts its priests. One nameless priest remains. He returns to his abandoned village church, where María Dolores, an unmarried mother whose child was fathered by the police lieutenant, finds him, and he baptises the village children in secret. The lieutenant takes hostages to force him into the open. The priest flees towards the port, shadowed by an informer and crossing paths with an American wanted for murder. Unable to say Mass without wine, he is arrested, unrecognised, with a bottle of brandy. Safe over the border, he goes back when a beggar brings a note, supposedly from the dying American, asking for confession. Captured, he refuses to renounce his faith and is shot. At the end another priest comes to the church to pray with the faithful.
inclusion: This is the most openly religious film John Ford made, and Steven Greydanus notes that Ford himself thought it his best. Gabriel Figueroa's black-and-white photography, shot on location in Taxco, Cholula and Cuernavaca, is its great strength. Henry Fonda plays the priest as a frightened man whose courage comes late, with Pedro Armendáriz as the lieutenant and J. Carrol Naish as the informer. Greydanus grades it A- and says that, though it softens Greene, it still packs spiritual punch; the debate between priest and lieutenant remains a high point. Its faults are real: Dennis Schwartz found it turgid and its religious symbols simplistic, and Bret Wood suggests the images are so striking that they distract from the priest's plight. It shared the International Award at Venice in 1948. As a parable of the persecuted Church and of a people's need for priests, it is direct rather than subtle.
themes: The film's subject is the sacramental priesthood under persecution. The priest baptises children who have had no priest for years. The plot turns on the Mass: without altar wine he cannot celebrate, and his search for it leads to his arrest. An informer betrays him, and he goes back across the border because a dying man may need a priest. Offered his life for apostasy, he refuses. His flaw in the film is pride in his office and fear, not the novel's drunkenness and fathered child. That makes him more conventionally edifying: Greydanus calls the result a softened, conventionalised Greene, and Schwartz thinks it loses the novel's moral urgency. The closing image of another priest arriving to pray states plainly that the Church outlasts its persecutors.
history: Graham Greene travelled in Mexico in 1938, when anti-clerical laws had closed churches and driven priests into hiding, and drew on that for his novel. Ford read it in 1940 but could not sell the project because of censorship problems. He and Merian C. Cooper made it for their company, Argosy Pictures, with RKO distributing. It was shot in Mexico with a largely Mexican crew and Emilio Fernández as associate producer, and released on 3 November 1947.
liberties: Greene's 'whisky priest' is an alcoholic who has fathered a child with María; the film makes the lieutenant the father and gives the priest only pride and fear. Greene's lieutenant is an idealist who wants to help the poor; Ford's is a harder tyrant. The setting is left unnamed rather than Mexico, and a spoken prologue presents the story as true.

title: Léon Morin, Priest
decision: REJECT: The subtitle file shows a heterodox thesis carried by the film's moral centre and never corrected. Explaining that there is no salvation outside the Church, Morin tells Barny she is not damned even if she goes on living as an atheist, and makes the Church an invisible Church of all humanity of goodwill, the reading Pius XII rejected in Mystici Corporis and Humani generis. In the closing conversation he asks why God should not work miracles for heretics, says God is Catholic only in our temporal language, and that the contradictions between the churches are mostly in our minds. Elsewhere he says the bourgeois distorted religion. With the sustained erotic focus already documented, this meets the rule against a heterodox thesis. Editor to confirm.
summary: Melville's Occupation drama of a Communist widow and a young priest whose arguments bring her back to a faith he recasts as an invisible Church of goodwill.
synopsis: A small Alpine town under the Occupation. Barny (Emmanuelle Riva), a widow whose Jewish husband has been killed, is a Communist and a lapsed Catholic bringing up her daughter alone and correcting work for a correspondence school. To mock the Church she goes to confession and baits the young priest, Léon Morin (Jean-Paul Belmondo), with the old line that religion is the opium of the people. He answers her, and she keeps coming back. Over months of private conversations she returns to the faith. Her feelings for him turn romantic, and other women of the town are drawn to him too; none succeeds in seducing him. When the Germans leave, the school returns to Paris and Morin is transferred to another parish. On his last night he sees her once more, tells her they will meet in another life, and she leaves in tears.
inclusion: Jean-Pierre Melville works here in a chamber register: most of the film is two people talking in small rooms, and it holds because the arguments are real. Belmondo plays a quick, blunt priest who questions authority and is not afraid of gossip; Dennis Schwartz found his case for God forceful and intelligent. Riva is the real centre, and even Eye for Film, otherwise cool on the film, praises her nuanced performance. Sean Axmaker in Video Librarian called it a solid chamber drama, respectful of the Church, with a priest who is chaste and devoted; the hosts of the Catholic film podcast Criteria call it one of the best priest films ever made and read it as a study in pastoral prudence. Not every critic agrees: Eye for Film found the theological exchanges grating and the story close to soap opera. It is talky and deliberately low-key. The difficulty is that the faith he argues for is not quite the Church's.
themes: The core is a conversion worked out through argument, and the argument is the problem. Morin answers Barny's Marxist jibes, but his answers reshape the faith: he tells her that no salvation outside the Church means an invisible Church of all people of goodwill, that she is not damned even if she remains an atheist, and at the end that God is Catholic only in human language and that contradictions between the churches are mostly in our minds. Nobody in the film corrects him. Barny's desire for Morin also grows with her faith, and though he keeps his vows and sends her away, he lets the private meetings run on for months.
history: Béatrix Beck's novel Léon Morin, prêtre won the Prix Goncourt in 1952 and was published in English as The Passionate Heart. Melville cut a first assembly of about three hours down to the 117-minute release; a longer director's cut of about 128 minutes was restored in 2019. The film drew 1.7 million admissions in France.
advisories:
Sustained romantic and sexual tension between a widow and a priest; no sex scene. The heroine is also shown as attracted to a female colleague.

Occupation setting, with the deportation of Jews in the background; reviews do not report graphic violence.

Adult in theme and slow in pace; for older teenagers and adults.

The priest teaches that an atheist need not be damned and that the Church is the invisible community of goodwill, and the film presents him as its moral centre. The heroine's conversion is entangled with her desire for him.

title: Going My Way
decision: PUBLISH: The AFI Catalog gives a full synopsis and production record; John Clark (NCRegister), Anthony Esolen and Joe Wilson give detailed Catholic readings of its portrait of parish priesthood. The Criteria critique and David E. White's scholarly chapter (the film nearly omits the supernatural and sacramental) are real limits and are stated in the record, but they describe an emphasis, not a teaching that contradicts the faith.
summary: Bing Crosby's easygoing young curate quietly takes over a debt-ridden New York parish from its stubborn old pastor, played to perfection by Barry Fitzgerald.
synopsis: St Dominic's, a poor New York parish, is about to lose its church to the mortgage holder. The bishop sends Father Chuck O'Malley, a former songwriter who wears a sweatshirt and plays golf, ostensibly as curate to the elderly Father Fitzgibbon, in fact to take charge without humiliating him. O'Malley turns a gang of street boys into a choir, helps a runaway girl, marries her to the landlord's son, and sells a song to pay the debt. Fitzgibbon learns the truth and runs away into the rain, then comes round. When the church burns, the parish starts again, and O'Malley moves on to the next troubled parish.
inclusion: McCarey made a comedy about two priests, and the comedy is real. Barry Fitzgerald's Fitzgibbon, crotchety, vain, devoted and finally touching, is one of the great character performances of the period, and his scenes with Crosby have an easy rhythm that holds the film together. Crosby underplays O'Malley's tact: he takes over without ever saying so. The film is long and loosely plotted, the opera interlude with Risë Stevens stops it dead, and the delinquents reform suspiciously fast. But its picture of a parish as a place where a priest knows the landlady, the policeman and the boys stealing turkeys has warmth and observation. The final scene, with Fitzgibbon's mother, is famous for good reason.
themes: The film's subject is the parish priest as a father to his people: patience with an older priest, care for the poor and the young, refusal to humiliate anyone. Esolen calls its governing virtue tact, a form of charity. John Clark draws out its respect for ordinary priestly service and a line affirming the indissolubility of a valid marriage. What it hardly shows is the supernatural centre of the priesthood. The scholar David E. White notes that it leaves out nearly all supernatural, sacramental and theological reference, and Thomas Mirus and James Majewski argue that O'Malley is admired for singing and charm rather than anything spiritual. That criticism is fair. Watch it as a portrait of priestly kindness, not of the priest at the altar.
liberties: Fiction; no historical persons. The parish is idealised and the plot runs on coincidence and a hit song.
advisories:
No violence beyond a church fire. A runaway girl lives in an apartment paid for by a young man before they marry; nothing is shown.

Suitable for all ages, though younger children may find it slow.

The priesthood is presented almost entirely through pastoral kindness; sacramental life is largely absent.

title: The Bells of St. Mary's
decision: PUBLISH: AFI Catalog record plus Stephen B. Earley's 1945 America review, which judged it 'tremendously spiritual' and among the best screen portraits of a sister's life, and Joe Wilson's detailed reading. The 'personable priest' critique (Criteria; White) applies more weakly here than to Going My Way because the sisters' vocation and prayer are central; it is noted in the record.
summary: Father O'Malley meets his match in Ingrid Bergman's Sister Benedict as a parish school fights to survive, in McCarey's warmer, more prayerful sequel to Going My Way.
synopsis: Father O'Malley becomes pastor of St Mary's, whose sisters run a crumbling parish school. The superior, Sister Mary Benedict, disagrees with him about almost everything, from school holidays to whether a struggling girl should pass her exams. She prays that the businessman Horace Bogardus will give the school the new building he is putting up next door; Bogardus wants the school site for a car park. O'Malley helps a deserted mother and her daughter Patsy, and nudges Bogardus towards charity. Bogardus gives the building. Then Sister Benedict is found to have early tuberculosis, and the doctor wants her transferred without being told why. She believes O'Malley has had her removed.
inclusion: This is the better of McCarey's two priest pictures, and the reason is Ingrid Bergman. Her Sister Benedict is strict, competitive, funny and devout, and she plays the part without condescension: Earley, writing in America in 1945, said sisters at an advance screening recognised themselves in her. The rivalry with Crosby's O'Malley is gentle comedy between two people who respect each other. Some scenes are pure McCarey: the infants' Nativity play, the nun teaching a bullied boy to box. It is sentimental and long, and the Bogardus subplot is contrived. But the last scene, in which Sister Benedict goes to the chapel to pray for guidance before leaving, and O'Malley finally tells her the truth, is beautifully done.
themes: The film takes religious life seriously. Sister Benedict's vocation is the teaching of children, and she holds to standards because she believes they serve the child. She prays for the school and the prayer is answered, though through a cranky businessman rather than a wonder. Her final trial is obedience: she accepts a transfer she does not understand and takes it to prayer before she knows the reason. O'Malley is still more pastoral counsellor than sacramental minister, and critics such as Thomas Mirus find the faith shallow; but here the sisters' prayer and obedience give it more spiritual weight than Going My Way.
liberties: Fiction. McCarey based Sister Benedict on his aunt, a sister of the Immaculate Heart community in Hollywood; Bergman's habit is a composite of two orders.
advisories:
A deserted mother says she has relied on 'the generosity of men', and her daughter mistakes her father for one of her mother's clients; this is handled discreetly.

title: Boys Town
decision: GREY: Identity and content are settled by AFI, the Legion of Decency's A-I (the pre-conciliar Catholic judgment), the 1938 Photoplay Studies guide and Simcha Fisher's review. The transcript shows two points the Founder should weigh: the film presents as an ideal a community where each boy worships as he pleases and a boy with no religion can stay that way, and it builds its message on the motto that there is no bad boy. It is not REJECT, because a priest acting under obedience is the centre and the lines describe the real institution's practice. It would be PUBLISH if the Founder judges this a charity's policy rather than indifferentism.
summary: Spencer Tracy won an Oscar as Fr Edward Flanagan, the Omaha priest whose town for homeless boys rests on his belief that there is no bad boy.
synopsis: Father Edward Flanagan visits a condemned man who blames the institutions that failed him as a boy, and resolves to reach boys before they go wrong. With his bishop's permission and a loan from a pawnbroker friend, he opens a home in Omaha, then builds a self-governing town for boys outside the city, kept afloat by appeals and debts. Whitey Marsh, a cocky young tough sent by his gangster brother Joe, sneers at the place, runs a cynical campaign for mayor and loses. He walks out, and the little boy Pee Wee, following him, is hit by a car. Whitey then stumbles into Joe's bank robbery and is wounded, and Flanagan shields him from the sheriff. In the end Whitey leads the boys to the gang's hideout, the robbers are captured, the publicity rescues Boys Town, and Whitey is elected mayor.
inclusion: Tracy's performance is the reason the film lasts: brisk, humorous and quietly obstinate. It won him his second Oscar in a row. Mickey Rooney, as Whitey, is energetic and often hammy, and Simcha Fisher, reviewing it recently, finds that the second half slides into melodrama. Norman Taurog shot parts of it at the real Boys Town with Flanagan as technical adviser, and it was one of the biggest hits of 1938. The Legion of Decency rated it A-I. It remains the best-known film portrait of an American priest at work among the poor. The opening, in which Flanagan sits with a man about to be executed, sets a pastoral tone the rest of the film mostly keeps.
themes: Flanagan is shown as a priest acting under obedience. He asks his bishop's permission, gives up the offer of a parish, and says he has nothing for the fight but faith. Prayer appears at meals and in Whitey's plea, in a church, for Pee Wee's life. Two things need weighing. The film's motto, that there is no such thing as a bad boy, leans towards blaming circumstance for sin, though Flanagan's insistence on discipline and responsibility qualifies it. And the boys explain that at Boys Town everyone worships as he pleases and a boy who is nothing can stay nothing. The film presents this as part of the ideal, and its dedication speaks of boys of every creed.
history: Edward Joseph Flanagan (1886–1948), an Irish-born priest of the Omaha diocese, opened a home for boys in Omaha in 1917 and later moved it to farmland west of the city, where it became the incorporated village of Boys Town. He took in boys of any race or religion. The 1938 study guide notes that the home had cared for over 4,400 boys by then. Flanagan is a Servant of God; his cause for canonisation has been opened.
liberties: Whitey, his brother Joe, the bank robbery and the condemned man Dan Farrow are invented. The film compresses twenty years into a short span. AFI records that its ending, which suggested the town's money troubles were over, was later blamed for a drop in donations, one reason MGM made a sequel.

A condemned man's last hour; a bank robbery and shooting; a small boy is hit by a car.

A boy is pranked in blackface, a period joke.

Suitable for most ages.

The film presents Boys Town's open policy on religion, including for boys with none, as an ideal.

grey.question: Boys Town is a warm portrait of a real priest, and the Legion of Decency rated it A-I in 1938. Two things deserve weighing. It presents as an ideal a community where each boy worships as he pleases and a boy with no religion can stay that way, and its famous motto, that there is no bad boy, leans towards treating sin as the product of circumstance. Readers can judge whether these describe a charity's practical policy or a quiet religious indifferentism.

title: Come to the Stable
decision: PUBLISH: Greydanus's review, TCM and the AFI Catalog establish a gentle comedy in which two French nuns' trust in providence and works of mercy drive the plot, with a sympathetic bishop. The sentimentality noted by Greydanus is disclosed.
summary: Two French nuns arrive in a Connecticut village determined to build a children's hospital with no money, in a gentle Fox comedy loosely based on the founding of Regina Laudis.
synopsis: Sister Margaret and Sister Scholastica arrive in Bethlehem, New England, on a snowy night, with a promise to keep: a children's hospital. They take shelter with Amelia Potts, an eccentric painter of religious pictures. They set their hearts on a hilltop owned by a gambler, Luigi Rossi, and on land next to a songwriter, Robert Mason, who wants peace and quiet. With prayer, persistence and some cheerful bending of the rules, they work on the bishop, the gambler and their reluctant neighbour. Not every scheme works, and the bishop worries about their judgment, but the hospital begins to take shape.
inclusion: Henry Koster's film is a well-made studio comedy with real affection for religious life. Loretta Young and Celeste Holm play the nuns with conviction rather than winks, and Elsa Lanchester is a delight as their painter friend. All three were Oscar-nominated, and the film received seven nominations in total. Steven Greydanus calls it sweet and uplifting, and also more conventional and sentimental than Lilies of the Field. The sisters sometimes get their miracle and sometimes look credulous and silly. That is about right. It is a warm Christmas-season film for the whole family rather than a serious study of a vocation.
themes: The sisters' faith is simple and direct. They pray for what they need and expect an answer, and the film plays this both as comedy and as sincere trust in providence. Their hospital is a concrete work of mercy. The bishop is portrayed sympathetically: he supports their mission but doubts their practical sense. Greydanus suggests the film leaves open whether God is testing their faith or teaching them prudence, and perhaps both. The Bethlehem setting and the Nativity imagery tie the story to Christmas.
history: Clare Boothe Luce, a recent convert, wrote the original story. It was based on the arrival in 1946–47 of two Benedictine nuns from the Abbey of Jouarre in France, Mother Benedict Duss and Mother Mary Aline Trilles de Warren, in Bethlehem, Connecticut. The painter Lauren Ford gave them hospitality, and a Protestant industrialist, Robert Leather, gave land. They founded the Priory of Regina Laudis in a disused factory; it later became an abbey. Fox negotiated with the nuns and church authorities before making the film.
liberties: The real foundation was a contemplative Benedictine monastery. The film turns it into an active order building a children's hospital, invents the gambler, the songwriter and other neighbours, and adds the comic set pieces. TCM notes the plot was changed partly to avoid needing the real nuns' rights.
advisories:
Nothing objectionable; suitable for children.

Some mild comic deception by the sisters.

title: Heaven Knows, Mr. Allison
decision: PUBLISH: The Legion of Decency rated it A-I (1956–57), the pre-conciliar Catholic judgment. Steven Greydanus (A−) and Dennis Schwartz (B+) describe its treatment. The earlier doubt about the novice's commitment is settled by the English subtitle track: she refuses Allison's proposal because her heart is 'given to Christ', explains that vows bind under pain of losing one's soul and can be lifted only by papal dispensation, and the film ends with her vocation intact.
summary: John Huston strands a Marine corporal and a young nun on a Japanese-held Pacific island; he falls in love with her, and she keeps her vocation.
synopsis: In 1944 Corporal Allison, a Marine cut off from his unit, drifts on a raft to a small South Pacific island. Its sole inhabitant is Sister Angela, an Irish nun not yet in final vows, stranded since the old priest she came with died. They fish, catch turtles and plan to sail for Fiji on his raft, until Japanese troops occupy the island and the pair hide in a cave. Allison raids the enemy camp for food and kills a soldier who finds him. He tells Angela he loves her and asks her not to take her vows; she answers that her heart already belongs to Christ. Later, drunk on Japanese sake, he frightens her into running out into the rain, and she falls ill. When the Americans attack, Allison disables the Japanese guns and is wounded. She walks beside his stretcher as the Marines carry him away.
inclusion: This is Huston working in the vein of The African Queen: two people, one setting, and a patient study of how they come to respect each other. Robert Mitchum gives one of his best performances as an orphaned, unschooled Marine, and Deborah Kerr, nominated for an Oscar, plays the nun with humour and backbone rather than sweetness. Oswald Morris's CinemaScope colour photography of Tobago, standing in for the Pacific, is handsome, and the raid on the Japanese camp is tense. The middle stretch is slow and the outcome predictable; Dennis Schwartz calls it lightweight but a small gem. Steven Greydanus notes that the film understands the Marine Corps better than the convent. It never cheats: the love is real, and so is her refusal.
themes: The drama is a vocation tested and kept. Sister Angela first appears praying the Hail Mary. She explains that final vows come only after years of probation, that breaking them would cost a religious her soul, and that only the Pope can grant a dispensation. When Allison proposes, she calls her profession a betrothal to Christ and shows him the ring she will exchange for a gold one at her vows. She wavers once, under the strain of the siege, wondering whether God means her to take them, and she asks him whether he is obeying God or his own wish to fight. Her prayer for him, a good man outside the Church, is simple and orthodox. The film sets her vows beside his loyalty to the Marines, which makes them look more alike than they are.
history: The film is based on Charles Shaw's 1952 novel, in which the heroine is already a nun. The AFI Catalog records that an earlier treatment, in which a laywoman disguised herself as a nun and fell in love with the Marine, was rejected by the Church's advisers, and that a revised story was approved in May 1954. Twentieth Century-Fox bought the rights later that year. It was shot in Tobago in 1956.

title: Lilies of the Field
decision: GREY: It is Catholic-centred: the nuns, their trust in Providence and a chapel for the Mass drive the plot. It won the OCIC (Catholic) award at Berlin in 1963 (AFI), a pre-conciliar Catholic film-office judgment, and Greydanus (+3) and Esolen establish its content. But the transcript confirms the point the earlier HOLD raised: the Baptist hero is presented at Mass as sent by 'the God of all faiths', the sisters learn and sing his spiritual, and the offer to teach him their Latin chant goes nowhere. Given the Founder's position on interreligious framing, that is a real question for the reader rather than grounds for PUBLISH. It is not REJECT: the film presents personal charity, not the post-conciliar Church or dialogue as a programme. The Legion of Decency rating was not found.
summary: Sidney Poitier won an Oscar as a Baptist handyman who builds a desert chapel for a group of refugee German nuns in Arizona.
synopsis: Homer Smith, a Black ex-serviceman drifting through Arizona, stops at a remote farm for water. It belongs to five nuns, refugees from East Germany, led by the formidable Mother Maria, who decides at once that God has sent him. She talks him into mending her roof, then into building a chapel for the local Mexican-American Catholics, who have only an outdoor Mass said by a travelling priest. Homer, a Baptist, works without pay, teaches the sisters English and takes a paid job to buy their food. He wants to build the chapel alone and clashes with Mother Maria's stubbornness; he leaves, comes back, and finally lets the townspeople help. The chapel is finished on the eve of its dedication. Homer drives off in the night as the sisters sing the spiritual he taught them.
inclusion: It is a small film, shot in two weeks around Tucson on a tiny budget, and it works through its two lead performances. Poitier is funny, proud and touchy, and he became the first Black actor to win the Oscar for best actor. Lilia Skala's Mother Maria is the richer part: an iron-willed refugee who trusts Providence completely and bargains like a peasant. Their battle of wills, fought in broken English and in duelling Bible verses, is the heart of it. Anthony Esolen stresses that it is not a sentimental film, and Steven Greydanus finds nothing objectionable in it. Jerry Goldsmith's score and the spiritual 'Amen' stay in the memory. The Mexican townspeople are thinly drawn, and the hard-drinking travelling priest is a stock joke.
themes: The Catholic side is solid. The sisters live by prayer and poverty, Mother Maria trusts God for every brick, and the whole plot exists to give a poor parish a place to celebrate Mass. The difficulty is how the film handles religion between Homer and the nuns. He skips Mass for what he calls a Baptist breakfast; the sisters learn his spiritual and sing it; Greydanus notes that Homer's suggestion that they teach him their Latin chant, the Tantum ergo, goes nowhere. At the outdoor Mass he is introduced to the congregation as sent by 'the God of all faiths'. The film treats the difference between Catholic and Protestant as a matter of temperament and breakfast.
advisories:
No violence, sexual content or bad language.

Suitable for all ages.

The film presents a warm religious exchange between a Baptist and Catholic nuns, and one line calls God 'the God of all faiths'.

grey.question: Lilies of the Field is plainly Catholic in its nuns, its Mass and its chapel, and it won a Catholic award at Berlin in 1963. The question is its religious friendship. The Baptist handyman is introduced at Mass as sent by 'the God of all faiths', the sisters learn and sing his spiritual, and the exchange never runs the other way. Readers can decide whether this is ordinary charity between neighbours or a gentle indifferentism that treats the creeds as interchangeable.

title: Fighting Father Dunne
decision: PUBLISH: The Legion of Decency rated it A-I (1947–48), the pre-conciliar Catholic judgment. Variety's review (12 May 1948) and The Exhibitor give independent contemporary accounts, and Bonnie Stepenoff's Missouri Encyclopedia entry settles the history. Its liberties (an invented condemned boy, a borrowing from Boys Town) are disclosed. The priest acts under his archbishop's authority, and the climax is the conversion of a condemned boy, so no doctrinal reservation arises.
summary: Pat O'Brien plays the St Louis priest who opened a home for homeless newsboys in 1906, in an affectionate RKO tribute that ends in a condemned cell.
synopsis: St Louis, 1905. Father Peter Dunne finds newsboys sleeping in packing cases and freezing on the streets, and resolves to house them. Archbishop Glennon gives his blessing but no money, so Dunne begs, borrows and bargains: a rented house, donated food, a pony and cart from a reluctant merchant. His boys fight rival newsboys for street corners, and a circulation manager's thugs harass them. Matt Davis, a hostile boy whose father is in prison, joins the home, quarrels with the others and leaves. Later, on the run after a break-in, he panics and shoots a policeman who wanted to help him. He is sentenced to hang. Dunne pleads with the governor and fails, but stays with Matt, who turns to God before his execution. Dunne goes back to his boys and carries on.
inclusion: It is a modest studio picture, and it borrows heavily from Boys Town, but it has a real subject and a lead who believes in it. Pat O'Brien, Hollywood's most familiar screen priest, plays Dunne as patient and practical rather than pious; Variety praised him in 1948 for making the priest warm and human. Much of the pleasure lies in the small tricks by which Dunne coaxes beds, food and transport out of the city. Charles Kemper, Una O'Connor and Arthur Shields supply the comedy. The pace is leisurely, the newsboys' feuds are routine, and the condemned-boy finale is melodrama. But the closing scenes give a priest's duty to a dying sinner its full weight, and the film keeps its sentiment in check.
themes: Dunne's charity is shown as a priest's work done under obedience. He asks the archbishop's permission, accepts that the diocese cannot pay, and keeps the home going by begging. The film's Catholicism is practical rather than theological, and for most of its length it shows little of the sacraments. Its heart is the ministry to the condemned boy at the end. Dunne fights for a reprieve, fails, and then prepares Matt to die reconciled to God. Variety's reviewer describes the boy turning to God on the eve of his hanging. The film does not pretend that love always spares a boy the consequences of his crime, which gives it more moral weight than many films of its kind.
history: Peter Joseph Dunne (1870–1939) was orphaned as a child and ordained in 1903 by Archbishop John Glennon of St Louis. In February 1906 he opened a shelter for homeless boys, and in 1907 it moved into a purpose-built home on Washington Avenue. Glennon gave him a lifelong commission to care for homeless boys, and he was made a papal chamberlain in 1927. The home ran until 2006, when it merged into Catholic Services for Children and Youth.
liberties: The historian Bonnie Stepenoff calls the film an affectionate tribute rather than a factual account, and notes how much it borrows from Boys Town. Matt's crime and execution are invented. A real former resident, Matthew Davis, sued RKO in 1950 for damage to his reputation and lost. The film dates the founding to 1905; the home opened in 1906.
advisories:
A boy shoots a policeman, and a condemned boy's last hours are the climax.

Street fights between newsboys; a horse is killed and a boy's leg is crushed.

Suitable for children of about ten and up, with the ending in mind.

title: Father Brown
decision: PUBLISH: The Legion of Decency rated it A-I (released in the US as The Detective; 1953–54 list), which is the pre-conciliar Catholic judgment. Movie Nation's review and the contemporary notices quoted by Wikipedia give an independent account of its treatment. The English subtitle track confirms the sermon on grace, the Friday clue, the priest staking the cross on Flambeau's soul, and the prodigal-son ending. No doctrinal problem was found.
summary: Alec Guinness plays Chesterton's mild London priest, who loses a precious relic to a master thief and then pursues the thief's soul across France.
synopsis: Father Brown, a small and untidy London parish priest, is caught one night by the police at an open safe: he is putting back money a parishioner stole. His bishop then sends him to Rome with the ancient cross of St Augustine, which the famous thief Flambeau has sworn to steal. Brown guesses that a fellow priest on the journey is an impostor, because he orders a ham sandwich on a Friday, but in the Paris catacombs the man knocks him down and takes the cross. In disgrace, Brown tells his superiors that he gambled the cross for Flambeau's soul. With the help of the widowed Lady Warren, he sets a trap at an auction and traces the thief to a ruined château in Burgundy, full of stolen art. The film ends in Brown's church, as he reads the parable of the prodigal son.
inclusion: Robert Hamer, who made Kind Hearts and Coronets, brings the same dry wit to a gentler story. Guinness is the reason to watch. His Brown is absent-minded, polite and immovable, and the film never makes fun of his faith. The comedy is good, especially the auction and a chase in which priest and thief empty a milk van together. Peter Finch makes Flambeau vain and likeable, and Joan Greenwood adds warmth. The plot is thin and the middle sags. Roger Moore of Movie Nation ranks it below Guinness's best comedies, and Variety thought the casting its main distinction. It is still one of the few films in which a priest's detective work exists to save a sinner rather than to punish him.
themes: The film's Catholic ideas are stated plainly. Brown's first sermon says that nobody is made simply good or bad, that God's grace is offered to everyone, and that it must not be presumed on. He spots the false priest because a priest would not eat meat on a Friday. Rebuked for losing the relic, he says he staked it on the thief's soul, and he tells Flambeau he wants both back. His method is patience and mercy, not arrest: he refuses to help the police jail a man whose sickness is in his soul. A fable about a woman lost for clutching her onion makes the point about possessions, and the closing reading of the prodigal son marks Flambeau's return.
history: G. K. Chesterton published 'The Blue Cross', the first Father Brown story, in 1910, and collected it in The Innocence of Father Brown (1911). Chesterton became a Catholic in 1922. Guinness was received into the Catholic Church in 1956, two years after the film, and Movie Nation notes that the role is said to have affected his spiritual life.
liberties: Only the opening idea comes from 'The Blue Cross'. In the story, Valentin of the Paris police trails Flambeau across London, Brown keeps the real cross safe by switching parcels, and he unmasks the thief because Flambeau, disguised as a priest, attacks reason, which Brown calls bad theology. The film lets Flambeau steal the cross and invents Lady Warren, the auction, the Burgundy château, the art collection and Flambeau's repentance. In Chesterton, Flambeau reforms only in later stories.
advisories:
A thief knocks the priest down; otherwise only comic theft and mild peril.

No sexual content or bad language.

title: El padrecito
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred and well documented, now including a full Spanish subtitle transcript: a young priest's ministry, with Mass, confession, baptism and papal social teaching at its centre. Not PUBLISH because several comic beats treat sacramental discipline lightly (a refused baptism, a boy told he need not confess because 'no one knows yet what sin is', indulgences offered in a bet, the Last Supper retold in Cantinflas's patter), and no contemporary Catholic rating or independent critical assessment of its treatment was found. Not REJECT: its social teaching is quoted from Leo XIII, Pius XI and John XXIII, and the film itself mocks the liturgical novelties the priest pretends to propose. A Mexican Legion of Decency or Spanish Catholic rating from 1964–65 would settle it.
summary: Cantinflas plays a young priest sent to help an old parish priest in a Mexican town, winning it over with dice, a bullfight and papal social teaching.
synopsis: Father Sebastián arrives in the small town of San Jerónimo el Alto to assist the elderly parish priest, Father Damián. Damián's sister Sara takes him for a usurper, and most of the town agrees. He refuses to baptise a baby under a name he finds ridiculous, plays dice for school supplies, dances in the bell tower and preaches a sermon that the municipal president takes as an insult. The local strongman, Don Silvestre, a professed atheist, tries to drive him out and sabotages a bullfight meant to pay for a clinic; Sebastián fights the bull himself. Accused of teaching Communism, he quotes the popes' encyclicals. He opens a school, wins the clinic's land from Don Silvestre at cards and helps Damián's niece with the strongman's son. When a visiting prelate comes to replace Damián, Sebastián poses as a wild innovator so that the old man can stay.
inclusion: This was Cantinflas's first priest role and one of his biggest late hits in Mexico and Spain, directed by his regular collaborator Miguel M. Delgado. The pleasure is his patter: the cantinflesque double-talk that turns a sermon or a confession into a comic routine. Ángel Garasa's gentle old Damián is a good foil, and the farewell has real warmth. Critics at the time found it moralising and unoriginal, typical of Cantinflas's later films, and at two hours it is long. The social argument is pointed for 1964: the priest opens a school, raises money for a clinic, and quotes papal encyclicals when he is accused of Communism. John Mraz reads the film as anti-political rather than revolutionary, and the ending is a private bargain, not a programme.
themes: Sebastián's faith is never in doubt. He says Mass, hears confessions, visits the dying and preaches, and when Sara calls his talk of fair wages Communism he answers with Leo XIII, Pius XI and John XXIII. The trouble is in the jokes. He refuses a baptism over a silly name, though Damián rightly says a sacrament is never refused. He tells a boy who dislikes confession that he need not go, since no one knows yet what sin is. He offers indulgences in a bet, and his Last Supper sermon, in Cantinflas's patter, calls Christ a revolutionary of goodness. The film does not endorse liturgical novelty: his promise of mariachis instead of bells is a ruse, and the prelate dismisses it.
history: The film was shot in January and February 1964, mostly in San Miguel de Allende, Guanajuato, which stands in for the fictional San Jerónimo el Alto. It opened in Mexico on 3 September 1964, while the Second Vatican Council was still in session. Some critics accused Cantinflas of mocking the priesthood; he answered that his message would be positive and Christian. A group of Latin American seminarians in Rome is reported to have written to thank him.
advisories:
A fist fight and a bullfight.

The priest gambles and drinks rum and brandy, played for laughs.

Jokes at the expense of confession, baptism and indulgences; a comic retelling of the Last Supper.

Long (about two hours). Suitable for older children with some explanation of the jokes about the sacraments.

grey.question: El padrecito admires its priest, but several of its jokes are at the sacraments' expense. Sebastián refuses a baptism over a silly name, tells a boy he need not confess because no one knows yet what sin is, offers indulgences in a bet, and retells the Last Supper as comic patter that calls Christ a revolutionary. Against this, his social teaching is quoted from Leo XIII, Pius XI and John XXIII, and the film mocks liturgical novelty. No Catholic rating from 1964 has been found; one would settle whether the comedy was judged irreverent.

title: Of Gods and Men
decision: REJECT: Scope (Founder ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's Catholic content is the post-conciliar Church, presented as normal or exemplary: the Tibhirine community's interreligious witness, culminating in a testament that speaks of Islam in the language of post-conciliar dialogue.
summary: Beauvois's patient drama about the Trappists of Tibhirine, who chose to stay with their Algerian village through the civil war of the 1990s, knowing it could kill them.
synopsis: In the Atlas mountains of Algeria, a small community of French Cistercian monks keeps the Hours, farms, sells honey and runs a free clinic for the Muslim village below. When an armed Islamist group murders Croatian workers nearby, the army offers protection and the government urges the monks to leave. The abbot, Dom Christian, refuses the soldiers without first consulting his brothers, and the community is split. On Christmas Eve armed men come to the monastery demanding medicine; Christian faces down their leader. Over the following months each monk has to decide whether to go home to France or remain. They vote, pray, quarrel and eat a last meal together. One night in 1996 men take most of them away into the snow.
inclusion: Few films show the ordinary texture of monastic life this exactly: the chanted Office, manual work, chapter meetings, a hard-pressed infirmarian. Lambert Wilson's Christian is clever and sometimes high-handed; Michael Lonsdale's Brother Luc, the old doctor, is gruff, funny and unshakeable. The drama is a vocational one. Men who have already given their lives to God must decide whether that gift includes staying put when staying may mean death, and the film lets their fear, doubt and slow agreement play out without speeches. Caroline Champetier's photography and the long passages of plainchant give it a slow, steady rhythm. The wordless last supper, built on faces and a piece of recorded music, is one of the great ensemble scenes of recent cinema. Steven Greydanus calls its picture of lived Christian faith more appealing than any dramatic feature of the previous quarter-century.
themes: Steven Greydanus counts fewer than 2,000 words of substantive dialogue from the monks, and much of it is Scripture, psalmody and liturgy: the Good Shepherd who does not abandon his flock, the Incarnation preached at Christmas, a Communion scene, Compline, the Paschal mystery behind their choice. The monks do not try to convert their neighbours, and the film presents their relationship with Islam as friendship and service. It does not claim that Islam saves or that all religions are equal. The closing testament is the point of real tension: Christian hopes to see 'his children of Islam' as God sees them, calls Algeria and Islam 'a body and a soul', and ends 'Insh'allah'. Read with the pre-conciliar teaching against indifferentism (Mortalium animos), these lines are ambiguous rather than heretical, and a viewer may legitimately dissent from them.
history: The monks of Notre-Dame de l'Atlas at Tibhirine were kidnapped in the night of 26–27 March 1996; seven were killed and two, who were not found, survived. The Armed Islamic Group (GIA) claimed the killings; later testimony that the Algerian army was involved remains disputed. The seven were beatified at Oran on 8 December 2018 with twelve other religious killed in Algeria between 1993 and 1996.
liberties: The film draws closely on the monks' writings and was made with advisers who knew the community, but conversations, the Christmas Eve confrontation and the last supper are dramatised. Christian's testament is shortened: Greydanus notes that the film drops the phrase about Muslims 'shining with the glory of Christ' and other passages, and judges the cuts were made for length. The deaths themselves are not shown.
advisories:
Brief graphic violence, including the murder of foreign workers, and a few disturbing images.

One obscene expression. Rated R in the United States; 15 certificate in the UK. Best for older teenagers and adults.

French and Arabic dialogue with subtitles.

The abbot's testament speaks of Islam in terms traditional Catholics may find too irenic; the film does not endorse religious indifferentism, but it does not argue against it either.

title: The Little World of Don Camillo
alternateTitles: Le Petit Monde de don Camillo
Il piccolo mondo di don Camillo
decision: PUBLISH: Jacques Lourcelles (Cinema Ritrovato programme note), contemporary reviews (Valobra in Rassegna del Film, Crowther in The New York Times, Offord in the Socialist Standard) and Cathopedia's scene list together document a comedy built on a priest's rivalry with a Communist mayor, the crucified Christ's rebukes, the sacraments and reconciliation. Edition differences (French version longer, including the attempted suicide) are disclosed.
summary: Fernandel's hot-tempered parish priest and Gino Cervi's Communist mayor feud, brawl and make peace in a Po Valley village, while Christ on the altar crucifix keeps the priest in line.
synopsis: In a small town on the Po plain after the war, the Communists win the local elections and Peppone becomes mayor. His rival is the parish priest, Don Camillo, a big man with big fists, who takes his grievances to the crucifix above the altar, and Christ answers him, usually with a rebuke. The two men clash over a new Casa del Popolo, a strike, a football match, a procession and the baptism of Peppone's son, whom the mayor wants to name after Lenin. Between quarrels they cooperate when the village needs them. Two young lovers from feuding families try to drown themselves, which forces both men to help. After a final brawl the bishop transfers Don Camillo to a mountain parish. Peppone forbids the town to see him off, but waits for him at the next station.
inclusion: Julien Duvivier and René Barjavel turned Giovannino Guareschi's newspaper stories into one of the most popular European films of the 1950s. Fernandel's elastic face and Gino Cervi's slow-burning mayor make an ideal comic pair. Jacques Lourcelles called Fernandel's mix of serenity and mischief superb, and Bosley Crowther praised its vigorous and amiable conflict. The film is episodic. Fabrizio Valobra, reviewing in 1952, found it fragmentary and sketch-like, with only the procession and the closing walk to the station showing Duvivier's real style. That is fair, but the episodes are well built, and the conversations with the crucifix give the comedy a moral centre.
themes: The crucifix is the film's conscience. Christ, voiced by Ruggero Ruggeri in the Italian version and Jean Debucourt in the French, regularly checks the priest's temper and vanity; in one scene he tells him to throw away the stick he means to use. Don Camillo submits, grumbling. The sacraments are taken seriously beneath the jokes. He insists on a proper Christian name at the baptism, but he baptises the child. He also blesses the Communists' new building. The film's argument is that a priest may oppose Communism with all his strength and still owe its members love and pastoral care. Its anti-Communism is comic, not hateful.
history: Guareschi, editor of the satirical weekly Candido, began the stories in 1946 and collected them as Mondo piccolo: Don Camillo (1948). They grew out of the bitter 1948 election campaign between the Christian Democrats and the Communist–Socialist Popular Front. Guareschi presented the Christ of the stories as the voice of his own conscience. The film was shot in Brescello, Emilia, and released in Italy in March 1952 and in France in June 1952.
liberties: The screenplay selects and links separate Guareschi stories into a loose chronicle. The Italian and French versions differ. The French cut is longer, extending the attempted suicide, the brawl, the football match and Signora Cristina's funeral, and adding a short exchange with a statue of Our Lady. The US version adds an English narration by Orson Welles.
advisories:
Fist fights and comic brawling, including by the priest.

Two young lovers attempt suicide by drowning (longer in the French version).

Political insults and threats played for comedy.

Suitable for families with older children.
