title: The King of Kings
decision: PUBLISH: AFI Catalog identity; Steven Greydanus's detailed Decent Films review, Charles Musser's Criterion essay and K. V. Turley's National Catholic Register piece establish a reverent Gospel film with a Eucharistic Last Supper, a reverent Our Lady and a careful handling of guilt for the Crucifixion. The invented Magdalene prologue, Protestant-default intertitles and one unscriptural intertitle are disclosed rather than disqualifying.
summary: DeMille's silent life of Christ opens as a lurid Hollywood spectacle, then settles into a surprisingly reverent Gospel film, with H. B. Warner's quiet Christ and a Resurrection in colour.
synopsis: Mary Magdalene, a rich courtesan, is told that her lover Judas has gone off after a carpenter from Nazareth. She drives out in a chariot drawn by zebras to win him back, meets Jesus, and is freed of seven devils. The film then follows Christ through healings, the call of the disciples, conflict with the Temple authorities and the Roman occupiers, and into Holy Week: the Last Supper, Gethsemane, Judas's betrayal, the trial before Pilate, the way of the cross and the Crucifixion, cut against Judas's suicide, with an earthquake that splits the Temple. The Resurrection follows, in colour.
inclusion: Greydanus calls it flawed but powerful, and that is fair. The first reel is pure DeMille: a half-dressed Magdalene, an orgy, zebras. Then the tone changes. H. B. Warner, past fifty and rather old for the part, gives Christ dignity and gentleness; his scenes with children, including one where he mends a child's doll, are the warmest in the film. DeMille's craft is formidable: the crowds, the lighting, the cutting between the Crucifixion and Judas's death, the storm that follows. Musser, in his Criterion essay, finds Warner's divinity rendered by lighting rather than acting and some of the halo effects kitsch, and he has a point. But for a silent epic it holds attention, and its seriousness about the Passion is unmistakable.
themes: The Last Supper is handled with reverence: Peter holds the chalice to his heart, while Judas crumbles the host and lets it fall, a clear sign that the film treats the Eucharist as sacred. Our Lady appears with dignity throughout. The intertitles are mostly from the King James Bible and the sensibility, as Greydanus says, is Protestant by default, but nothing in it attacks Catholic belief. Turley objects to one intertitle in which Mary urges her Son to go back to Nazareth, which is unscriptural. On the Crucifixion, the film places guilt on Caiaphas as a Roman appointee and has him plead that he alone is guilty, a deliberate attempt to avoid blaming the Jewish people.
liberties: The opening, with Mary Magdalene as a courtesan and Judas's lover, is invented. Events are rearranged thematically: episodes about taxes are merged and crowd scenes moved. Caiaphas's final prayer is DeMille's invention. The 1927 roadshow version (about 155 minutes) and the 1928 general release (about 112) differ; the longer cut adds an exorcism and other material but also puts the opening in colour, which weakens the colour Resurrection.
advisories:
The opening shows a decadent party and a scantily dressed Magdalene; it is brief.

The scourging and Crucifixion are restrained by modern standards; Judas's suicide is cut against the Crucifixion; earthquake and storm.

Silent with intertitles. Greydanus rates it suitable for children and up, with these caveats.

title: The Nun's Story
decision: PUBLISH (adults and older teens): The AFI Catalog and Greydanus's Decent Films review show a serious, largely respectful account of pre-conciliar religious formation whose heroine leaves by lawful dispensation after judging herself unable to keep obedience, not a film that attacks the vows. Zinnemann deliberately withholds a verdict on her departure (AFI: no end-title music for that reason); Greydanus calls it neither anti-religious nor anti-Catholic. The film's ambiguity about whether the Rule or the nun is at fault is recorded plainly in the text and advisories.
summary: Audrey Hepburn plays a Belgian surgeon's daughter who becomes a nursing sister, serves in the Congo, and after years of struggle with obedience asks to be released from her vows.
synopsis: In the 1920s Gabrielle Van der Mal enters a nursing order in Bruges, hoping to serve in the Congo. As Sister Luke she learns the Rule: silence, custody of the eyes, obedience to the bell. Her superiors test her pride; one even urges her to fail an exam as an act of humility. She is sent to an asylum, then at last to the Congo, where she works beside a brilliant, irreligious surgeon and falls ill with tuberculosis. Recalled to Belgium, she faces the German occupation. Ordered to show charity to the enemy, she secretly helps the Resistance, and when her father is killed she finds herself full of hatred. Concluding that she can no longer be a true nun, she asks for release, signs the papers, changes into a dress and walks out of the convent.
inclusion: No Hollywood film before or since has shown the formation of a religious so carefully. The first hour, which the New York Times likened to a documentary, explains the vows through the words of superiors, and the rituals of the novitiate are filmed with patience. Hepburn is superb, entirely inward; Edith Evans is formidable as a superior, and Peter Finch plays the atheist surgeon who tells her she is a 'worldly nun' and that her real illness is the struggle to conform. Franz Planer's photography of Bruges and the Congo is beautiful. The film is long and its second half loses some of the first half's concentration. It is not a happy story. But it treats the religious life as a real and serious calling, and its sisters include warm and holy women as well as harsh ones.
themes: The film is about obedience. Sister Luke's struggle is not with faith in God but with the surrender of her will: leaving a dying patient at the sound of the bell, accepting humiliation, forgiving the men who killed her father. The Rule is presented in its own terms, and the superiors explain why the sacrifice of liberty matters. Greydanus notes that the bad advice to fail an exam is later corrected by another superior. The Congo scenes include a priest serving lepers in penance for his sins, and a sister murdered by a man in thrall to a witch doctor, whose fellow nuns' forgiveness draws villagers to the Christmas Eve service. Where the film is open to question is its refusal to judge the outcome: it never settles whether the fault lies with the Rule, the community or Sister Luke herself, and some viewers will read her departure as liberation. Read faithfully, it is the story of a vocation honestly found wanting, not of a vocation exposed as false.
history: Kathryn Hulme's 1956 novel was based on Marie-Louise Habets, a Belgian nursing sister who left her order during the Second World War; Hulme met her among refugees in 1945. The film was shot in Rome, Belgium and the Belgian Congo, including a leper settlement, and a real Congo missionary played Father André.
liberties: Names and some events are fictionalised from Habets's life by way of Hulme's novel. The Resistance episodes and the doctor's role are shaped for drama. The order is not named in the film.
advisories:
A violent attack in a mental asylum and a murder in the Congo; wartime bombing; scenes in a leper colony.

No sexual content, but unspoken attraction between the nun and the surgeon.

The heroine leaves religious life at the end, and the film does not say whether she was right. Greydanus rates it for adults; it suits mature teens with discussion.

title: Barabbas
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (Christ, St Peter, the Roman martyrs), Legion of Decency A-II (Motion Picture Exhibitor Legion tables, 1962), independent reviews (Hannan, Cinefile). Reservation: the hero's faith stays ambiguous to the end, and his doubt of the Resurrection and his part in the burning of Rome are the core of the story; Peter's rebuke and the martyrs' witness keep it from contradicting doctrine. Would move to PUBLISH if the Founder accepts an ambiguous convert as protagonist. The English subtitle file confirms the rebuke (the fire is Nero's, not God's, 02:11:56–02:12:40) and Peter's consolation that Christ has never left Barabbas's side (02:13:44–02:13:59); the last words are addressed into the dark without naming God (02:16:23–02:16:35).
summary: Anthony Quinn's Barabbas, freed in Christ's place, spends twenty years haunted by the man who died for him, in Richard Fleischer's grim and intelligent epic.
synopsis: Pilate offers the crowd Jesus or Barabbas, and they choose Barabbas. Freed, he finds that his lover Rachel has become a follower of the condemned man. He watches the Crucifixion under a darkened sky, finds the tomb empty and refuses to believe; Rachel preaches and is stoned. Back at his old trade, he is caught and sent for life to the sulphur mines of Sicily, chained to Sahak, a Christian. An earthquake frees them, and they are taken to Rome to be trained as gladiators. Sahak is executed for his faith; Barabbas wins his freedom in the arena. When Rome burns he thinks the end of the world has come, sets fires himself and declares himself a Christian. In prison St Peter tells him Christians do not do such things. He is crucified with the Christians.
inclusion: Barabbas is the most searching of the epics of its era. Dino De Laurentiis made it in Italy with real ambition: Christopher Fry wrote the script from Pär Lagerkvist's novel, and Brian Hannan reports that the darkness over Calvary was filmed during an actual eclipse. Anthony Quinn plays a slow, bewildered man who keeps failing the people around him, and Hannan rightly calls the performance excellent and the film overlooked. Fleischer keeps piety at arm's length; the mine, the arena and the burning of Rome are brutal and convincing. The dialogue can be stiff, and David Clare at Cinefile finds it a Christian-era Spartacus without that film's vision. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.
themes: The film is about grace resisted and, at the last, half understood. Barabbas lives because Christ died, and he cannot escape that fact. Rachel, Sahak and Peter are clear witnesses; Barabbas is not. He doubts the Resurrection, mistakes the fire of Rome for the end of the world, and joins in the arson for which the Christians are blamed. Peter's rebuke is plain: the fire is Nero's work, not God's. In prison Peter tells him that Christ died for him because he was farthest away, and has never left his side. Barabbas dies on a cross among the martyrs, giving himself up 'into your keeping' in the dark, without saying to whom. Catholic Culture's Criteria podcast calls him an archetype of human resistance to grace.
history: The Gospels record only that Barabbas, a prisoner held for insurrection and murder, was released instead of Jesus; everything after is invention. Lagerkvist, a Swedish Nobel laureate, published his novel in 1950. The film opened in Italy on 23 December 1961 and was released in the United States by Columbia in October 1962.
liberties: Barabbas's later life is wholly invented. Against the novel, the film sends him to Sicilian sulphur mines rather than copper mines in Cyprus, frees him by an earthquake rather than a sympathetic overseer, and adds the gladiatorial scenes.
advisories:
Brutal violence: a stoning, a mine disaster, gladiatorial combat, the burning of Rome and mass crucifixions.

Barabbas's relationship with Rachel is implied.

For teenagers and adults. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

The hero's faith is left ambiguous, and he takes part in the burning of Rome believing he serves the Christians.

grey.question: Barabbas is a film about a man who cannot believe. He doubts the Resurrection, helps set fire to Rome in the belief that he is serving the Christians, and dies on a cross with words that may be faith or only surrender. The martyrs around him, Rachel, Sahak and St Peter, are drawn with conviction, and Peter corrects his error plainly. The film's power lies in that ambiguity. Viewers who want a clear conversion story will not find one; those willing to watch a portrait of resistance to grace will.

title: Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ
originalTitle: Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ
decision: GREY: Identity is secure (AFI Catalog, BFI) and the treatment is established by Greydanus (moral/spiritual +3, Kids & Up*), who calls it arguably the best version of the story. Christ is shown reverently, never with his face, in Technicolor sequences framing the drama: the Nativity, the cup of water, the raising of a child, the healing of the lepers on the way of the cross, the Crucifixion. Two reservations stop it at PUBLISH: Christ is the background to a revenge melodrama from a Protestant novelist rather than its centre, and the restored version contains brief nudity (bare-breasted women in a procession, a nude galley slave) that censors cut in 1931.
summary: MGM's silent Ben-Hur sets Lew Wallace's revenge tale inside the life of Christ, from a Technicolor Nativity to the Crucifixion, with a still-astonishing sea battle and chariot race.
synopsis: The film opens in Bethlehem with Joseph and Mary, the birth in the cave, the shepherds and the Magi. Years later in Jerusalem, Judah Ben-Hur, a Jewish prince, is betrayed by his Roman boyhood friend Messala; Judah is sent to the galleys and his mother and sister are imprisoned. On the road a young carpenter of Nazareth gives him water. Judah survives a sea battle, wins his freedom and returns to defeat Messala in the chariot race. He gathers men to fight for the foretold king, but the Nazarene, carrying his cross, heals Judah's mother and sister of leprosy, and before the Crucifixion Judah lays down his sword when Christ speaks of a kingdom not of this world.
inclusion: This was the most expensive silent film ever made, shot partly in Italy and finished in California, and it still looks it. Greydanus judges the sea battle the best of any version and the chariot race at least equal to the 1959 remake; Kevin Brownlow compared the race to the Odessa Steps in Potemkin. Ramon Novarro plays Judah, and at around two and a half hours it is an hour shorter than Wyler's version and better paced; Greydanus notes that it delays the rescue of Judah's mother and sister, which helps the drama. The Christ scenes were shot in two-strip Technicolor, considered lost until the 1980s and restored in 1987, so the Gospel episodes literally glow against the tinted story. Photoplay singled out Betty Bronson's Madonna.
themes: Christ is never seen full-face; he is a hand, a figure, a presence, and the title cards quote the Gospels. That restraint is the film's best religious decision. The Nativity is staged with Mary and Joseph at the centre and treated with reverence. Judah's journey moves from vengeance towards Christ: he plans an army for a political Messiah and learns at the foot of the cross that the kingdom is not of this world. Greydanus approves of keeping the Gospel in the background, but notes that Hollywood's melodramatic spectacle sits uneasily with sacred subjects. The novel's author, Lew Wallace, was a Protestant, and the faith in the film is a broad, undogmatic Christianity.

grey.question: Christ appears in Ben-Hur with real reverence, in the Nativity, the healing of the lepers and the Crucifixion, but the film belongs to Judah's revenge and the chariot race, and its faith is the general Christianity of Lew Wallace's novel rather than anything specifically Catholic. The full restoration also includes brief nudity cut by censors in 1931. Viewers will want to decide whether a spectacle in which Christ is the frame, not the subject, belongs alongside films about Him.

history: Lew Wallace, a Union general, published Ben-Hur in 1880; it became one of the best-selling American novels of the century. MGM's production began in Italy under Charles Brabin, who was replaced by Fred Niblo, and was completed in Culver City. It premiered in New York on 30 December 1925. A shortened reissue with synchronised music followed in 1931.
liberties: Judah, Messala and the Ben-Hur family are Wallace's inventions. The film follows the novel's main line but ends at the Crucifixion, whereas the novel continues into the reign of Nero. Christ's words and the healing of the lepers are placed on the way of the cross for dramatic effect.
advisories:
Battle violence at sea, galley brutality and the chariot race crash.

Brief partial nudity (women in a procession, a galley slave) and a sequence of mild sensuality.

The Crucifixion is shown without graphic detail.

Greydanus rates it Kids & Up with these cautions; better for older children.

title: Ben-Hur
alternateTitles: Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ
decision: PUBLISH: Christ is the hinge of the drama (Crowther, 1959: Judah's emergence from hatred is achieved through the example and teachings of Jesus), so it qualifies under the Bible-epic rule despite its Protestant-authored source; nothing in it contradicts Catholic teaching. Legion of Decency A-I (Motion Picture Exhibitor Legion tables); independent treatment from Crowther (NYT review reprinted in Motion Picture Exhibitor) and Greydanus; identity from AFI.
summary: Wyler's epic of a Jewish prince betrayed by his Roman friend, whose hatred is finally dissolved at the foot of the Cross; the grandest of Hollywood's biblical films.
synopsis: Judea, AD 26. Judah Ben-Hur, a wealthy Jewish prince, welcomes back his boyhood friend Messala, now a Roman tribune. When Judah refuses to inform on his countrymen, Messala seizes on an accident to send him to the galleys and imprison his mother and sister. On the march to the coast a carpenter in Nazareth gives the parched Judah water. Years later Judah saves the life of the Roman commander Arrius in a sea battle, is adopted as his son, and returns to Judea seeking revenge. He beats Messala in the chariot race; the dying Messala tells him that his mother and sister are lepers. Embittered, Judah follows the condemned Jesus to Calvary, recognises the man who gave him water, and tries to give Him water in turn. At the Crucifixion his mother and sister are healed, and Judah's hatred leaves him.
inclusion: It is the summit of the Hollywood biblical epic. The chariot race, staged by Andrew Marton and Yakima Canutt with Charlton Heston and Stephen Boyd doing much of their own driving, remains one of the great action sequences, and the film won eleven Academy Awards. Steven Greydanus notes that it does not transcend its genre of spectacle and melodrama, but does those things about as well as they could be done. Bosley Crowther in 1959 thought it the most stirring of all the Bible-fiction pictures and singled out Judah's meetings with Jesus as dignified and true. Its weaknesses are length and stiffness, and Greydanus finds Judah's loss of faith once his fortunes improve hard to follow.
themes: The subtitle is A Tale of the Christ, and Wallace's design holds. Christ appears only at the edges of the story, His face never seen and His voice never heard, yet every turn of Judah's life passes through Him. The water given at Nazareth is returned on the road to Calvary. The healing of the lepers comes with the death on the Cross, and Greydanus points to the image of Christ's blood running into the rain that washes the hillside. Judah's conversion is from vengeance to forgiveness rather than a full confession of faith, so the religious meaning is real but understated. The Nativity, the Sermon on the Mount and the Passion are treated with reverence.
history: Lew Wallace published Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ in 1880, and it had been filmed in 1925. MGM's remake was shot at Cinecittà in Rome in 1958–59 on a budget of about $15 million; the producer, Sam Zimbalist, died during the shoot. It opened in New York on 18 November 1959.
liberties: Judah, Messala, Arrius and their families are fictional, from Wallace's novel. Judah's meetings with Jesus, the water given and returned, and the healing of the lepers at the Crucifixion are invented around the Gospel scenes, in keeping with Wallace's design.
advisories:
Battle and arena violence: the sea battle and the chariot race, with a trampled, mangled charioteer.

The lepers' disfigurement; the scourging and Crucifixion are shown with restraint.

Suitable for older children and up; the length, over three and a half hours, is the main obstacle for the young.

The Legion of Decency rated it A-I.

title: Black Robe
decision: GREY: Identity and content are well established (Australian Screen curator's notes, Video Librarian, the Lehigh 'Reel American History' scene log, Wikipedia). No Catholic review was found. The reservation is real but can be weighed: an ambivalent, partly sceptical view of the mission from Brian Moore's script, a priest who questions whether an unbaptised friend is lost, and several on-screen sex scenes that pre-conciliar standards would not pass. Not REJECT because the priest's faith and endurance are treated with respect and the film ends in an act of charity and a baptism. The Founder may prefer REJECT on the sexual content. The English subtitle file shows that Laforgue does not deny that the unbaptised are lost: he anguishes over it in prayer ('Why is Father Jerome with you in Heaven while Chomina lies forever in utter darkness?', 01:28:30). He baptises a dying child, makes his confession to a fellow priest, refuses to present baptism as a cure, and baptises the Hurons at the end after they ask whether he loves them. That strengthens GREY rather than REJECT.
summary: Bruce Beresford's austere adaptation of Brian Moore's novel follows a young Jesuit through the winter wilderness of New France in 1634, testing his faith against an alien world.
synopsis: In 1634 Samuel de Champlain sends Father Paul Laforgue, a young Jesuit newly arrived in New France, to a distant mission among the Hurons. He travels by canoe with a party of Algonquins led by Chomina, together with Daniel, a young Frenchman who falls in love with Chomina's daughter Annuka. Laforgue, shaken by desire and by the Algonquins' ways, does penance in the forest. A shaman calls him a demon and the party abandons him; Chomina, ashamed, turns back. An Iroquois war party then captures them, kills Chomina's wife and young son and tortures the prisoners until Annuka helps them escape. Chomina dies without accepting baptism. Laforgue reaches the mission alone and finds the Hurons dying of fever. Asked whether he loves them, he says yes, and baptises them.
inclusion: Black Robe is one of the few films to take seventeenth-century missionaries seriously on their own terms. Moore drew on the Jesuit Relations, and the film is often cited for the care of its research into Algonquin and Huron life. Peter James's photography of the wilderness won awards in Canada and Australia, and the film took six Genie awards, including best picture and best direction. Lothaire Bluteau plays Laforgue as an inward, uncertain man; Randy Pitman of Video Librarian found him a bit of a cipher who cries a lot and says little. Roger Ebert, quoted by later writers, praised its realism but was left depressed by the ending. The case for it is that Laforgue is no caricature. He endures cold, hunger, contempt and torture to reach his mission, and the last scene is a baptism. The difficulty is that the film keeps its own view of that mission at a distance.
themes: The film turns on a missionary's vocation under pressure. Laforgue holds to prayer, the sacraments and the conviction that the unbaptised are lost, and the film tests all three. He baptises a dying child, flogs himself after watching Daniel and Annuka together, and confesses to a fellow priest. Chomina refuses baptism because his people will not be in the Christian paradise, and Laforgue later asks God why a dead priest is in heaven while Chomina lies in utter darkness: grief at the doctrine, not denial of it. He will not offer baptism as a cure for fever, but baptises the Hurons when they ask whether he loves them. The Algonquins' dream-world is given as much weight as his faith, and the ending can be read as charity or as defeat.
history: Moore based his 1985 novel on the Jesuit Relations, the annual reports that missionaries in New France sent to their superiors, and the Australian Screen notes add Francis Parkman's history as a source. Laforgue and his companions are fictional. The closing title is broadly historical: the Huron missions were destroyed by Iroquois attacks at the end of the 1640s, and the surviving Jesuits withdrew to Quebec.
liberties: Laforgue, Daniel, Chomina and Annuka are invented, and the journey is a composite of episodes from the Relations. The film's portrait of Indigenous life is widely praised for its research, but Ward Churchill criticised historical inaccuracies and its portrayal of the Mohawks.
advisories:
Several sex scenes: a couple in a shared lodge, Daniel and Annuka in the woods, and Annuka seducing a guard to free the prisoners.

Graphic torture and killing by an Iroquois war party, including the killing of a child, an arrow through the neck and a severed finger.

A priest flogs himself.

Rated R in the United States; for adults.

The film's view of the mission is ambivalent, and the priest's anguish over an unbaptised friend is left unresolved.

grey.question: Black Robe takes a Jesuit missionary seriously, gives him the sacraments and ends with a baptism, but it keeps its own judgment of the mission at arm's length. It sets the priest's faith beside the Algonquins' dream-religion as near equals, lets him cry out to God over an unbaptised friend he believes lost, and closes on the destruction of the Christian Hurons. It also contains several sex scenes and graphic torture. Viewers who know the Jesuit Relations and the story of the North American Martyrs can weigh how much of the film's ambivalence is honesty and how much is scepticism.

title: Brideshead Revisited
decision: GREY: Identity is secure (ACMI; Wikipedia credits and broadcast record) and fidelity is documented (Sturridge's 95 per cent claim; Spectator 2021 retrospective; Seeing Things Secondhand episode review). The Catholic thesis is Waugh's and orthodox: deathbed absolution and the sign of the cross, Julia's renunciation, Charles before the sanctuary lamp. The reservation is moral, not doctrinal: brief nudity and an intimate scene (the 'bottoms' debate recorded by the Spectator), a long adulterous affair and a homoerotic undercurrent. The editor may judge this PUBLISH with advisories, as with Diary of a Country Priest; it is not REJECT, because the story judges the sins it shows.

grey.question: The serial keeps Waugh's Catholic argument whole: a dying man returns to the sacraments, a woman gives up the man she loves rather than live in sin, and an unbeliever ends on his knees. To make that argument it shows the sins at length: an adulterous affair over several episodes, brief nudity and an intimate scene, and a romantic friendship between two young men that some critics at the time thought overplayed. The question is whether what is shown along the way is acceptable for the sake of an ending that judges it.

summary: Granada's eleven-part, near-verbatim adaptation of Waugh's novel, in which an agnostic painter is drawn, through his love for a Catholic family, towards the faith that divides them.
synopsis: In wartime, Captain Charles Ryder's company is billeted at Brideshead, and the house brings back his past. At Oxford in the 1920s he befriends Lord Sebastian Flyte, charming and evasive, and is drawn into the life of his Catholic family: the devout, possessive Lady Marchmain; her estranged husband, living in Venice with his mistress; and their children Bridey, Julia and Cordelia. Sebastian sinks into drink, escapes abroad and ends as a hanger-on at a North African monastery. Years later Charles, now an unhappily married painter, begins an affair with Julia, who is married to the divorced Rex Mottram, and they plan to divorce and marry. Lord Marchmain comes home to die. He sends the priest away, but at the last accepts absolution with the sign of the cross. Julia breaks with Charles. In 1943 Charles prays in the reopened chapel.
inclusion: Granada's serial is often named the finest literary adaptation British television has made; Anthony Burgess called it the best piece of fictional television ever made, and it won the BAFTA for best drama series. Its distinction is fidelity. Charles Sturridge said 95 per cent of the dialogue is Waugh's, and Jeremy Irons's narration carries long stretches of the prose. Laurence Olivier's dying Lord Marchmain is the dramatic peak, and John Gielgud's dry Mr Ryder is a comic treasure. Length is the obvious weakness: eleven episodes, some static, and contemporary critics such as Richard Ingrams found it too long and the score too insistent. Because it keeps nearly all of Waugh, it keeps the novel's Catholic argument intact, including the parts that secular viewers in 1981 found hardest to accept.
themes: The novel's subject is grace working on very different people, and the serial keeps it. Each of the Flytes is caught by the 'twitch upon the thread' in a different way: Sebastian in drunken exile beside a monastery, Lord Marchmain at his deathbed, Julia when she gives up the man she loves rather than set up a rival good to God, and Charles, the sceptical narrator, who ends praying before the relit sanctuary lamp. The faith is shown as costly and inconvenient, and Lady Marchmain's possessive piety does real harm. Sin is not softened: adultery, divorce, drunkenness and the romantic friendship of the two young men are shown at length, and judged by the end rather than along the way.
history: Evelyn Waugh, a convert since 1930, published the novel in 1945. Granada first planned a six-hour serial. A strike halted filming, Michael Lindsay-Hogg left for another commitment, and Charles Sturridge completed it at eleven episodes (659 minutes). John Mortimer's script was set aside and the producer, Derek Granger, built the screenplay from Waugh's text, though Mortimer kept the credit. ITV broadcast it from 12 October to 22 December 1981, and PBS from January 1982.
liberties: Very few. Descriptive detail is cut and the narration lifts whole passages of Waugh's prose. The serial makes visible, briefly, things the novel only implies, such as the young men sunbathing naked on the roof.
advisories:
Brief rear male nudity (two young men sunbathing on a roof) and a scene in which Charles touches Julia's breast.

An adulterous affair across several episodes, with the couple living together; divorce.

The Charles and Sebastian friendship has a romantic undercurrent; a scene in a gay nightclub.

Heavy drinking and alcoholism.

For older teenagers and adults.

The religious resolution comes only in the last episodes; viewers who stop midway see the sin without its judgement.

title: Christus
decision: GREY: Identity is secure (Silent Era; Wikipedia citing Pucci 2016; cinemaitaliano.info) and the content is a Life of Christ and of Our Lady built from tableaux after Fra Angelico, Leonardo and Michelangelo, with Leda Gys as the Madonna. The Vatican helped send it into Germany in 1917, which shows contemporary Church favour but is not an assessment of its treatment. No independent review describing the film's handling of the Gospel was found. It would move to PUBLISH with a substantive review or scholarly description of the restored print (Cineteca di Bologna 2000), or a contemporary Catholic notice.
summary: Cines' four-year Life of Christ, shot partly in Egypt and Palestine, stages the Gospel as a series of living pictures after Fra Angelico, Leonardo and Michelangelo.
synopsis: Christus tells the life of Christ from the Annunciation, staged after Fra Angelico, through his childhood (Renato Visca plays Jesus at twelve) and public ministry to the Passion. Leda Gys plays the Virgin Mary and Amleto Novelli plays Pontius Pilate; Alberto Pasquali plays Christ and Augusto Mastripietri plays Judas. The Last Supper is staged as a living reproduction of Leonardo's fresco, placed at the centre of the film. Michelangelo's Pietà, Mary holding her dead Son, is among the works of art the film reproduces. The scenario, by Antamoro and Ignazio Lupi, follows a poem by Fausto Salvatori, and parts of the film were shot at the places of the Passion. The surviving version was reconstructed from fragments held in archives abroad.
inclusion: Christus was the first Italian epic of the life of Christ and an international hit; it premiered in Paris at the Trocadéro with an orchestra, and Wikipedia quotes Pucci calling it a milestone of Italian religious epic cinema. Antamoro spent four years on it and took his crew to Egypt and Palestine. Its method is pictorial: rather than invent a cinematic style, it brings famous religious paintings to life, which places it in the tradition of the Pathé Passion and of sacred art. Leda Gys, then a leading Italian star, plays the Madonna. The film was nearly lost after the arrival of sound and was reconstructed and restored in 2000, shown at Venice with a new score by Mgr Marco Frisina. How well the reconstruction plays as a whole has not been reviewed in any source found.
themes: The film's Catholic character lies in its sources. It takes its images from the great Catholic painters of the Annunciation, the Last Supper and the Pietà, so that Mary is present at the Annunciation and in the Pietà, and the institution of the Eucharist is given the central tableau. Salvatori's poem frames the Gospel as a sacred narrative rather than a historical reconstruction. During the First World War the Vatican helped bring the film into Germany through Switzerland. No source found describes the intertitles or how particular doctrines are presented.

grey.question: Christus is a Life of Christ built from Catholic sacred art, with the Annunciation after Fra Angelico, the Last Supper after Leonardo and a Pietà after Michelangelo, and the Vatican helped distribute it in 1917. What is missing is an independent account of how the restored film handles the Gospel: its intertitles, its miracles and its Resurrection. A detailed review of the 2000 Bologna restoration, or a contemporary Catholic notice, would settle it.

history: Giulio Antamoro worked on Christus for Cines from 1912 to 1916, shooting partly in Egypt and Palestine and partly in Italy. It opened in Italy in November 1916 and in the United States in April 1917. It was a commercial success until the coming of sound, after which prints disappeared. It was reconstructed from fragments in several archives, restored by the Cineteca di Bologna with Titanus, the company of Leda Gys's son Goffredo Lombardo, and shown at Venice in 2000.
advisories:
Passion scenes staged in tableau form; no graphic violence is reported.

Silent; the restored version has a modern score by Marco Frisina.

title: Conspiracy of Hearts
decision: PUBLISH: Catholic-centred in that a community of nuns and its charity are the subject. Legion of Decency A-I and a detailed contemporary trade review (Motion Picture Exhibitor, 16 March 1960: 'a reverent, potent drama'); identity and production history from Wikipedia and the Exhibitor credits. The English subtitle file shows the one romantic thread is the Italian major's courting of a novice, who rebuffs him; the Mother Superior counsels her soundly about her vocation, and refuses on the ground of the sisters' vows to let him kill to save them. Nothing there unsettles PUBLISH.
summary: Lilli Palmer's prioress and her nuns smuggle Jewish children out of an internment camp beside their Italian convent in 1943, in a well-made British weepie.
synopsis: Northern Italy, 1943. Beside a convent stands a camp where Jewish children are held under Italian guard. Mother Katharine and her nuns smuggle the children out, hide them and pass them on to safety. Major Spoletti, the Italian commander, hates the job and looks the other way. Not every sister agrees: Sister Gerta fears for the community. Then the Germans take over the camp, and Colonel Horsten and his zealous lieutenant Schmidt tighten the watch and investigate the escapes. A rabbi is caught leading a secret Yom Kippur service for the children in the convent cellar and is shot. The Germans raid the convent and condemn Mother Katharine and two sisters to death. The Italian firing squad fires over their heads, the Germans are killed, and the Italian soldiers leave to join the partisans.
inclusion: The film was among the most popular at the British box office in 1960, and it holds up as solid, emotional studio filmmaking. Lilli Palmer is the reason to see it. Motion Picture Exhibitor thought her performance worthy of an Oscar, called the film reverent and heart-rending, and singled out the cellar service as the scene to remember. Sylvia Syms and Yvonne Mitchell give good support as a young sister and a doubting one. David Parkinson of Time Out is less kind, calling it a synthetic weepie, and the plotting is conventional, with stock German villains and a last-minute rescue. It was shot partly at the Certosa di Galluzzo near Florence and at Pinewood. The Legion of Decency rated it A-I.
themes: The sisters act as nuns. Their charity to the children grows out of their religious life, and the drama turns on what a community is prepared to risk for strangers. Mother Katharine's authority, Sister Gerta's prudence and the younger sisters' courage give a fair picture of obedience under pressure. A subplot has the Italian major court the novice Mitya; she rebuffs him, and the Mother Superior tells her not to force herself into religious life if her heart is elsewhere, sound counsel to a novice. At the climax the Mother forbids him to kill a German to save them, because the sisters live by the law of God they promised to keep. The rabbi's Yom Kippur service, ended by German bullets, is the most remembered scene.
history: The story is invented. It began as a 1956 American television play for the Goodyear Playhouse, set in 1946, about nuns helping Jewish children reach Palestine. Its real author was the blacklisted screenwriter Adrian Scott, writing under the name of his friend Dale Pitt; Robert Presnell Jr. wrote the screenplay, which moved the story to 1943. Betty Box produced it for Rank.
advisories:
Wartime menace: executions are threatened, a rabbi is shot, and several Germans are killed at the end.

Children in danger throughout.

An Italian officer courts a novice, who turns him away; nothing more.

Suitable for older children and up. The Legion of Decency rated it A-I.

title: Loyola, the Soldier Saint
decision: PUBLISH: Pablo Úrbez Fernández's scholarly study (Trasvases entre la literatura y el cine 4, 2022), based on the Spanish censorship files, establishes a near-complete and largely faithful life of St Ignatius, from his youth at court to his death in Rome in 1556, drawing on his Autobiography for Pamplona, the Montserrat vigil, the encounter with the Moor, Manresa, the Paris companions and Montmartre. A Jesuit, Fr Carlos María de Heredia, was adviser. The liberties (an invented infanta, an invented antagonist and his mistress, a strong militarist-patriotic colouring) are disclosed. Wikipedia gives identity; no doctrinal problem is reported.
summary: A Spanish biopic of St Ignatius from courtier and soldier to founder of the Jesuits, faithful to his Autobiography but coloured by the military patriotism of 1940s Spain.
synopsis: Íñigo leaves Loyola as a boy for the Castilian court, grows into an idle young gallant who dreams of the Infanta Catalina, and enters the service of the Duke of Nájera. Made captain, he leads the defence of Pamplona against the French in 1521 and is struck down by a cannonball. Convalescing at Loyola, he asks for books and is given lives of St Francis and St Dominic; his brother Martín warns him against vague dreams. He leaves for Montserrat, keeps vigil and lays down his arms before Our Lady, and on the road argues with a Moor who denies Mary's virginity, letting his mule decide whether to pursue him. He lives in prayer at Manresa and Barcelona. In Paris he meets Francis Xavier, is accused of heresy over his Exercises, and founds the Society at Montmartre. In Rome he converts the scoffer Beltrán and dies in 1556.
inclusion: Unlike most saint films of its day, this one covers almost the whole life, and Úrbez shows how closely it follows Ignatius's own Autobiography in the episodes that matter most: the reading at Loyola, the armour laid before the Virgin of Montserrat, the comic and revealing incident of the Moor and the mule, Manresa, the meeting with Xavier. Rafael Durán plays Íñigo. The production was serious: a Jesuit adviser, a censor's report praising the dialogue, and José María Pemán's name on the script, though Úrbez notes Pemán supplied only a short outline. It is also a document of its time. Contemporary provincial reports were mixed, criticising the Pamplona scenes and calling the direction inexperienced and the ending forced. The Roman section turns to fiction to illustrate Ignatian spirituality through the conversion of an invented sinner.
themes: The spine of the film is conversion: the gallant who reads the lives of the saints and resolves to outdo them, the knight who keeps vigil before Our Lady and gives up his sword, the penitent of Manresa. A censor summed up its thesis as conquering the passions through the Spiritual Exercises. Our Lady's virginity is defended in the Moor episode, and the founding of the Society is a Mass at Montmartre celebrated by Peter Faber. In Rome Ignatius sends his men out to defend the Church against heresy and carry the Gospel to the Indies. Úrbez notes that the film fuses soldier and saint more than conversion strictly allows, and that its title cards include 'war against the enemies of God'.
history: Íñigo López de Loyola (1491–1556), a Basque nobleman, was wounded at Pamplona in 1521 and converted while convalescing. He kept vigil at Montserrat in March 1522, lived as a penitent at Manresa, where the Spiritual Exercises took shape, studied at Alcalá, Salamanca and Paris, and with six companions took vows at Montmartre in 1534. The Society of Jesus was approved in 1540. He died in Rome on 31 July 1556 and was canonised in 1622.
liberties: The Infanta Catalina as Íñigo's ideal lady is invented, and the film makes him eight when he leaves home rather than sixteen. It makes him leader of the Pamplona defence. The tavern brawl and the shipwreck he providentially misses in Barcelona are invented. Jerusalem, Alcalá, Salamanca and Venice are skipped. The Roman section is largely fiction, built around Beltrán and his mistress Marcelilla.
advisories:
Battle violence at Pamplona; Íñigo's wound.

An invented sinner keeps a mistress in the Roman section; no explicit content is reported.

The film presents Ignatius in strongly military and Spanish-nationalist terms typical of its period.

Suitable for older children and adults.

title: From the Manger to the Cross
originalTitle: From the Manger to the Cross
alternateTitles: From the Manger to the Cross; or, Jesus of Nazareth
decision: GREY: Identity and content are well established (AFI Catalog; Greydanus, moral/spiritual +3, Kids & Up). The reservation is the film's shape: Greydanus describes it as Protestant in sensibility, built on King James title cards, with the Baptism of Christ left out, Mary's part at Cana removed and no Resurrection; it ends at the death of Christ with John 3:16. Nothing is contrary to faith, but the omissions are real and a reader can weigh them. It would move to PUBLISH if the Founder judges a Life of Christ ending at Calvary acceptable when the omission is disclosed.
summary: Kalem's Life of Christ, shot in Palestine and Egypt in 1912, has striking real locations and reverent staging, but stops at Calvary without the Resurrection.
synopsis: The angel's message comes to Mary, though the angel himself is never seen. Joseph is shown struck by a light from outside the frame. Christ is born in Bethlehem, the Magi and shepherds come, and the Holy Family flees into Egypt, filmed in front of the real Sphinx and pyramids. Scenes of the boy Jesus in Nazareth follow. John the Baptist points out the Lamb of God, though Christ is only a distant figure. The disciples are called, and the ministry includes the wedding at Cana, healings and the raising of Lazarus. The Passion follows from the Last Supper to the Crucifixion. Most of the title cards are verses from the King James Bible. The film closes with the death of Christ and a final card quoting John 3:16.
inclusion: Sidney Olcott and Gene Gauntier took a Kalem unit to the Holy Land in 1912 and filmed where the events took place. That alone makes the film unusual: the hills of Galilee and Nazareth are real, and the flight into Egypt passes the Sphinx, an image Greydanus thinks later films should have copied. Costumes follow James Tissot's watercolours of the life of Christ. The Annunciation, with Mary addressed by an angel we never see, is simply and memorably done. The acting is more natural than in earlier Passion films, but the pace is slow, and the reliance on long Bible quotations makes it a reading film as much as a visual one. The National Film Preservation Foundation ranks it as the most important silent film about Christ, and the Library of Congress added it to the National Film Registry in 1998.
themes: The film treats the Gospel with reverence: Christ is played with restraint and the Passion is not sensationalised. Greydanus, though, calls its approach Protestant, relying on the scriptural text to speak for itself rather than on the visual tradition of the Church. The omissions follow from this. Christ's Baptism is never shown. At Cana, Mary does not bring the shortage of wine to her Son, so her intercession, which Catholic tradition draws from that scene, is lost. Above all there is no Resurrection: the story ends with Christ's death and a verse about God's love.

grey.question: This is a reverent and in places beautiful Life of Christ, but it is shaped by a Protestant reading of Scripture. It leaves out Christ's Baptism, cuts Mary's request at Cana, the Gospel basis of her intercession, and ends at Calvary with John 3:16, so the Resurrection never appears. Nothing in it contradicts the faith; the question is whether a Gospel film that stops at the Cross gives a true account of the Gospel. Greydanus pairs it with Pathé's Life and Passion for the Resurrection and Ascension.

history: Kalem sent Olcott's unit to Palestine and Egypt in 1912. The film opened in London on 3 October 1912 at Queen's Hall before an audience of clergy and in New York at Wanamaker's Auditorium. The Daily Mail asked whether nothing was sacred to filmmakers, but the clergy found little to object to. Vitagraph reissued a re-edited version after 1919, and the Rev. Brian Hession re-released it in 1938 with music and spoken commentary.

title: Ida
decision: GREY: Identity (Danish Film Institute, Wikipedia) and content (Globe and Mail and Time Out, independent; Catholic Herald, Aleteia and US Catholic, content only) are established. Reservations: a novice sleeps with a man before her vows, the ending leaves her profession open, and the film draws a parallel between a parish priest's certainty and a party official's (US Catholic). Not REJECT because the pre-conciliar convent and the vocation are treated with respect and the film argues no anti-Catholic thesis.
summary: Paweł Pawlikowski's spare black-and-white film about a Polish novice who learns, days before her vows, that she was born Jewish and her family murdered in the war.
synopsis: Poland, 1962. Anna, an orphan raised by nuns, is about to take her vows when her superior sends her to meet her only relative, her aunt Wanda, a hard-drinking judge who was once a Stalinist prosecutor. Wanda tells her she was born Ida Lebenstein, a Jew. The two drive into the countryside to find where her parents are buried. They learn that Feliks Skiba, whose family had sheltered the Lebensteins, killed them, and killed Wanda's small son too. Ida gives up any claim to the farm, and the two rebury the bones in a Jewish cemetery. Back in the city, Wanda jumps from her window. After the funeral Ida tries her aunt's life: she drinks, smokes, dances with the young saxophonist Lis and sleeps with him. He offers marriage and an ordinary life. At dawn she puts her habit back on and walks away.
inclusion: Ida won the Academy Award for best foreign-language film, the first Polish film to do so, and its reputation rests on its form: black-and-white images, long, still takes and very little dialogue. It runs eighty minutes and wastes none of them. Agata Kulesza's Wanda, worldly, sardonic and broken, is the performance critics singled out, and Agata Trzebuchowska, a newcomer, is all stillness; Kiva Reardon in the Globe and Mail calls her masterful. Reviewers compared the film to Dreyer and Bresson. For Catholic viewers its interest is that a film of this standing takes a novice's vocation seriously, sets it in a pre-conciliar convent of Latin prayer and silent meals, and does not mock it. Mark Judge at Aleteia called it the kind of film Catholics say is never made any more. It is also bleak, and its ending can be read more than one way.
themes: The convent is shown plainly: the nuns pray in Latin, eat in silence and work, and Anna kneels at a wayside shrine and blesses an infant. Wanda's taunt that Jesus did not hide from the world puts the film's question: is Anna's vocation a flight or a choice? Her night with Lis is the film's answer, of a kind. She tries the world, and in the morning goes back to the habit. Pawlikowski does not show whether she makes her profession. Patrick McCormick in US Catholic notes an unsettling parallel between the certainty of the parish priest and that of the party official. The guilt of Polish villagers in Jewish deaths is at the film's centre, and some Poles objected to it.
history: Many Jews in occupied Poland survived by hiding with Polish families, and some were betrayed or killed by those who sheltered them; Poles who helped Jews also risked execution. Ida's story is fictional. A petition signed by more than 40,000 people asked for title cards stating that thousands of Poles were executed for helping Jews; the producer, Eric Abraham, refused.
advisories:
A novice sleeps with a man before returning to the convent; her aunt's casual affairs are shown.

A suicide.

The exhumation of murdered family members, including a child.

Rated PG-13 in the United States; for older teenagers and adults.

grey.question: Ida is a serious, respectful film about a novice in a pre-conciliar Polish convent, and it does not mock her faith. But the decisive episode before her vows is a night in which she drinks, dances and sleeps with a musician, and the film leaves open whether she goes back to make her profession. Some viewers will see a soul choosing God with open eyes; others, an ambiguity the film never resolves. It also draws a parallel between a priest's certainty and a communist official's. Viewers can weigh both.

title: Bernadette of Lourdes
decision: PUBLISH: Catholic-centred life of St Bernadette (canonised 1933). Identity from Unifrance, Cinema Belgica and eofftv; independent treatment from Stuart Galbraith IV (DVD Talk, 2008, via the Wayback Machine); Legion of Decency A-I (Motion Picture Exhibitor Legion tables, 1962). Year 1961: French release 4 February 1961, after Belgian censorship in December 1960 and a Variety review in September 1960.
summary: A modest French life of St Bernadette, scripted by the Catholic novelist Gilbert Cesbron, that keeps the Lady unseen and follows Bernadette from the grotto to the convent at Nevers.
synopsis: Lourdes, 1858. Bernadette Soubirous is the eldest child of a destitute family, asthmatic and slow at her lessons with the sisters, but given to answers of surprising depth. Gathering wood by the river with her sister and a friend, she sees a lady in the grotto of Massabielle. The secret gets out and the town takes sides. The curate believes her; the parish priest, Abbé Peyramale, and the Bishop of Tarbes are slower to be convinced. The imperial police and magistrates question her and forbid her to go to the grotto, and her own family joins them. The apparitions continue: the spring appears, and the Lady names herself the Immaculate Conception. To shield her from the crowds the Church sends her to the sisters at Nevers, where she lives out her life hidden, ill and serving others.
inclusion: It is worth seeking out as the sober French counterpart to The Song of Bernadette. Gilbert Cesbron wrote the script, and Danièle Ajoret looks right as Bernadette. Stuart Galbraith IV, reviewing the American DVD, finds its approach more poetic and less literal than the Hollywood film: the Virgin is neither seen nor heard, only suggested, as in The Miracle of Our Lady of Fatima. He is equally clear about its faults: a tight budget, too many scenes of people talking about events instead of showing them, a restless zoom lens, and a jaunty score that undercuts the drama. The only American DVD is a soft English dub, slightly shorter than the original. The Legion of Decency rated it A-I.
themes: The apparitions are treated as real, and the film follows the Church's own sequence: the parish priest's and the bishop's caution, the test of asking the Lady's name, and the answer, the Immaculate Conception, which Galbraith notes the unschooled girl could hardly have known. The emphasis falls on Bernadette's simplicity and obedience. The title, 'It is enough to love', points to the last part, where her vocation at Nevers is shown as hidden suffering and service rather than glory. Beyond the spring, no miracles are shown, partly for want of money, so the weight falls on her witness.
history: Bernadette Soubirous (1844–79) saw eighteen apparitions at Massabielle in 1858. In 1866 she entered the Sisters of Charity at Nevers, where she died. She was canonised in 1933. The film was passed by the Belgian censors in December 1960 and opened in France on 4 February 1961; Janus Films first distributed it in the United States.
advisories:
Nothing objectionable. Illness and poverty are shown plainly.

Suitable for all ages. The Legion of Decency rated it A-I.

title: Joan the Woman
decision: GREY: Identity and content are established (AFI Catalog; Giornate del Cinema Muto 2019 note by Anne Morey; Movies Silently review). St Joan was canonised in 1920, so no hard rule applies. The reservations are concrete: an invented English lover, Eric Trent, whose betrayal leads to her capture; a First World War frame in which Joan's ghost urges a soldier to a suicide raid to atone for English sins; and a film more interested in Joan as patriot and woman than as saint. Not REJECT because her mission, visions and martyrdom are treated with respect; not PUBLISH because the inventions change the meaning of her story.
summary: DeMille's lavish 1916 epic of Joan of Arc, framed by the First World War trenches, has fine battle scenes and Handschiegl colour, and an invented English lover.
synopsis: In a French trench in 1916 an English officer, Eric Trent, finds an old sword in the earth and dreams of Joan of Arc. In the fifteenth-century story, his ancestor, also called Eric Trent, raids Joan's village of Domrémy, is wounded and is hidden and nursed by Joan, who is fond of him. Her visions then call her to the Dauphin, and she sets him aside. She persuades Charles, leads the French army, raises the siege of Orléans and sees Charles crowned. Trent, now an English commander, captures her at Compiègne and tries to ransom her, but his actions help her enemies. Bishop Cauchon tries her for heresy and she is burned at Rouen. In the trench Joan's spirit appears and tells the officer to expiate English wrongs; he volunteers for a night raid on the German lines and is killed.
inclusion: This was DeMille's first historical epic and one of the most expensive American films of its day. Its strengths are visual: storybook sets and costumes, clearly staged battles at Orléans, and the burning at Rouen tinted in red and yellow by the new Handschiegl process. Anne Morey's note for the 2019 Pordenone restoration describes Joan as a sturdy, honest country girl shown in Christ-like images, crucified in the shadow of the fleur-de-lis, and surrounded by men who are cruel, weak or cowardly. Geraldine Farrar, the opera star, is uneven: Movies Silently finds her strong in quiet and combat scenes but stiff in the visions and the trial, and Leonard Maltin thought her miscast. Raymond Hatton's Charles VII is a standout. It is worth seeing for its scale and for comparison with Dreyer and Gastyne.
themes: Joan's visions send her on her mission and she follows them faithfully; once called, she never looks back at Trent. Her death at the stake is presented as martyrdom, and Morey notes the film's repeated Christ-like imagery around her. But the film's centre of gravity is elsewhere. It treats Joan chiefly as a patriot and a woman, as the title says, and its romance and wartime frame turn her into a sponsor of Anglo-French alliance. The ghost who urges a soldier to die to atone for her death is an invention with no basis in her life or in Catholic teaching on expiation. The trial judges, in white pointed hoods, are villains.

grey.question: DeMille honours Joan's courage and her death, but he reshapes her story. He invents an English lover whose betrayal causes her capture, and he wraps the film in First World War propaganda: Joan's ghost urges a modern soldier to a suicidal raid to atone for her burning. The voices are treated respectfully but briefly; the film's real subject is Joan as patriot and woman. Viewers who know the history can enjoy the spectacle; those wanting her sanctity should start with Dreyer.

history: Joan of Arc (c. 1412–1431) heard the voices of St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret, raised the siege of Orléans in 1429 and saw Charles VII crowned at Reims. She was captured at Compiègne by Burgundian forces in 1430, sold to the English, tried for heresy at Rouen by a court under Bishop Pierre Cauchon and burned on 30 May 1431. She was rehabilitated in 1456, beatified in 1909 and canonised in 1920.
liberties: Eric Trent and the romance are invented; Joan was captured by Burgundians, not betrayed by an English lover. The modern frame is wholly fictional. DeMille and Jeanie Macpherson drew on Schiller's play and Mark Twain's novel rather than the trial records. The film was cut from eleven reels to eight soon after release, and the French version dropped the English frame.
advisories:
Battle violence and the burning of Joan at the stake, tinted in colour.

An attempted seduction in Domrémy; no nudity reported.

A soldier is sent on what amounts to a suicide mission at the urging of Joan's ghost.

Older children and up; long (about 140 minutes restored).

title: King of Kings
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred life of Christ. The reservation is documented by contemporary Catholic evidence: the Legion of Decency gave it a Separate Classification (Motion Picture Exhibitor Legion tables, 1962; AFI: 'taking poetic license with the life of Christ'), while the Vatican's Catholic Cinematographic Centre later gave it its highest classification. Invented Zealot subplot, political Judas, reduced role of the Sanhedrin. Not REJECT: no heterodox thesis; not PUBLISH because of the Legion reservation.
summary: Nicholas Ray's life of Christ, with Jeffrey Hunter, sets the Gospel inside a Zealot revolt and makes Judas a disappointed rebel: handsome, reverent and freely rewritten.
synopsis: Narrated by Orson Welles, the film opens with Pompey's capture of Jerusalem in 63 BC and the Roman occupation. Jesus is born in Bethlehem, escapes the massacre of the innocents and grows up in Nazareth. Meanwhile Barabbas and Judas lead Zealot raids against Pilate. Jesus is baptised by John, tempted in the desert, gathers the apostles and preaches the Sermon on the Mount, and Judas leaves Barabbas to follow Him, hoping He will lead the revolt. Herod Antipas has John beheaded. Barabbas launches a Passover rising, and Pilate's legions crush it. Judas, wanting to force Jesus' hand, betrays Him. Pilate condemns Him and releases Barabbas, and Judas hangs himself. After the Crucifixion the risen Christ speaks to the apostles by the sea, His shadow falling in the shape of a cross on the fishing nets.
inclusion: Samuel Bronston's production is handsome: shot in Spain in 70mm, with a Miklós Rózsa score and a long Sermon on the Mount staged as an exchange with the crowd. Ray's widescreen compositions are often striking. Jeffrey Hunter's Christ is gentle and remote, and Siobhán McKenna's Mary is dignified. The critics divided. Time called it the corniest, phoniest Bible story of the decade, while Variety and Harrison's Reports praised it. DeCine21 finds it respectful and faithful to Scripture in many respects, though drawn as much from Tacitus as from the Gospels; Cinefile, more enthusiastic, calls it the most satisfying film of the Passion of its time but notes its liberties. The Legion of Decency gave it a Separate Classification.
themes: The film affirms the Nativity, the miracles, the Passion and the Resurrection, and it treats Christ with reverence. Its problem is emphasis. Long stretches belong to Barabbas and the Zealots, and Judas betrays Christ to force Him into leading a revolt, a modern theory with no basis in the Gospels. The part of the Jewish authorities in the Passion is reduced and Rome made chiefly responsible; John Farrow left the project rather than make that change. Christ's divinity is stated more than dramatised, and Richard Coe complained that the film made Him uncontroversial. Vatican reviewers rated it highly; the American Legion objected to its poetic licence.
history: Pope John XXIII reportedly received Bronston and approved the script in 1960. Philip Yordan wrote the screenplay, and Ray Bradbury wrote the narration. Shooting took place mainly in Spain in 1960, with reshoots in December 1960 and in London in 1961. The film opened in New York on 11 October 1961.
liberties: The Zealot revolt led by Barabbas, Judas's political motive, Christ's visit to John the Baptist in prison and the Roman centurion Lucius, who follows Christ's career, are invented. The Sanhedrin's role is minimised and Pilate's enlarged. The Resurrection is shown only by a shadow and a voice.
advisories:
The massacre of the innocents, the beheading of John and battle scenes; the scourging and Crucifixion are restrained.

Suitable for older children and up.

The Legion of Decency gave it a Separate Classification for its liberties with the life of Christ.

grey.question: King of Kings is reverent, but it rewrites the Gospel in significant ways. Much of its running time goes to an invented Zealot rising; Judas betrays Christ to provoke a revolt; and the part of the Jewish authorities in the Passion is played down so that Rome bears the guilt. The Legion of Decency, finding that it took poetic licence with the life of Christ, gave it a Separate Classification rather than one of its ordinary ratings. Viewers who know the Gospels well can enjoy its images while setting its inventions aside.

title: The Saint Who Forged a Country
originalTitle: La virgen que forjó una patria
alternateTitles: The Saint That Forged a Country
decision: GREY: Identity and content are established (Wikipedia citing Rodríguez and BAMPFA; a detailed credits-and-plot page reproducing Jesús Ibarra's commentary; UnoTV). The core is Catholic: the evangelisation of New Spain, a friar's defence of the Indians, and the 1531 apparitions to Juan Diego with the miraculous image presented to Bishop Zumárraga. The reservation is the frame: the story is told by Fr Miguel Hidalgo to justify taking Our Lady of Guadalupe as the banner of armed insurrection, and the film closes on that banner. Hidalgo was excommunicated by his bishop in 1810; the film presents his use of the image approvingly. Juan Diego was beatified only in 1990 and is a character, not the subject (rule (a) does not apply; he must not be called saint or blessed). Not REJECT because the apparitions are central and reverently told.
summary: Julio Bracho's Guadalupe film has Fr Hidalgo, on the eve of revolt in 1810, recount the conversion of Mexico and the apparitions to Juan Diego, played by Ramón Novarro.
synopsis: Querétaro, September 1810: Hidalgo, Allende and the other conspirators plan a rising against Spain and Hidalgo chooses the Virgin of Guadalupe as its banner. When the plot is discovered, Hidalgo tells Allende how the Virgin came to Mexico. In 1528 the Spaniard Pedro de Alonso enslaves and brands Indians, and the Aztec noblewoman Xochiquiahuit, who has taken up with him, is rejected by her father. A friar, Fray Martín, opposes the abuses, baptises the weaver Cuauhtlatoa as Juan Diego and brings Alonso to court; Alonso's own child is born branded, and he blinds himself and dies. Fray Martín wins from Charles V a school for Indians at Tlatelolco and dies on the voyage home. In 1531 the Virgin appears to Juan Diego on Tepeyac, and her image appears on his cloak before Bishop Zumárraga. The film returns to 1810 and the insurgents raise her banner.
inclusion: This is one of the most ambitious religious films of Mexico's golden age, photographed by Gabriel Figueroa with music by Miguel Bernal Jiménez, and it gave Ramón Novarro, the silent star of Ben-Hur, a late role as Juan Diego. The commentary reproduced from Jesús Ibarra praises Bracho's direction, the cast, especially Novarro, and Jorge Bustos's editing, which binds the two periods together. It was less successful than Bracho's previous two films, and a recent programme note calls it an icon of Mexican kitsch, love it or hate it. Its interest lies in the colonial half: the clash between the conquistador and the friar, the founding of the college at Tlatelolco and a careful, reverent staging of the Tepeyac apparitions and the image on the tilma. The 1810 frame is talky and patriotic.
themes: Our Lady of Guadalupe is presented as the Mother who unites Indian and Spaniard in one faith: the apparitions come after the friar's fight against slavery and the first baptisms, and the image on Juan Diego's cloak persuades the bishop. The Church is shown on the side of the Indians against the conquistador, and the miracle is treated as real. The problem is the frame. The film makes the apparition the foundation of Mexican nationhood and ends with a priest raising the image as the standard of a revolt that his bishop condemned. Devotion and insurgent nationalism are run together without comment.

grey.question: The heart of this film is a reverent telling of the Guadalupe apparitions and the conversion of Mexico. But the whole story is framed as Fr Miguel Hidalgo's justification for taking Our Lady's image as the banner of the 1810 insurrection, and the film ends on that banner. Hidalgo was excommunicated by his bishop that year. Viewers should know that the film presents the Virgin of Guadalupe as patroness of a priest-led revolt and treats this as her purpose.

history: Catholic tradition holds that in December 1531 Our Lady appeared four times to the Indian convert Juan Diego on the hill of Tepeyac, and that her image appeared on his tilma before Bishop Juan de Zumárraga. The cult was approved and the image crowned in 1895; Pius X named her patroness of Latin America in 1910. On 16 September 1810 Fr Miguel Hidalgo began the war of independence at Dolores and took up a Guadalupe banner at Atotonilco; the Bishop-elect of Michoacán excommunicated him that month.
liberties: Fray Martín, Pedro de Alonso, Xochiquiahuit and their story are invented to dramatise the conquest and evangelisation. The link between the apparitions and the independence movement is the film's thesis, not history; one critic calls the historical frame a pretext for justifying the Guadalupe banner, and commentators note errors in the colonial and 1810 sections.
advisories:
The branding and enslavement of Indians; a man blinds himself.

An unmarried liaison between a Spaniard and an Aztec woman; a child born of it.

The frame presents the 1810 insurrection, led by a priest later excommunicated, as the fulfilment of the apparition.

title: Lourdes and Its Miracles
decision: PUBLISH: Catholic-centred documentary on Lourdes. Identity from Unifrance (Fiches du Cinéma synopsis) and French Wikipedia; independent treatment from Jean Collet (Encyclopædia Universalis), who calls it the most honest and moving document on the Lourdes pilgrimages; the National Legion of Decency rated the US release A-I (1958–59).
summary: Georges Rouquier's three-part documentary on Lourdes: cures examined by the Medical Bureau, a pilgrim's day of devotions, and two sick women filmed before and after their cures.
synopsis: The film is built as three linked short documentaries, narrated by Rouquier himself. The first, 'Témoignages', opens on the commercial bustle of the town and then examines three cures recorded by the Bureau des constatations médicales: a nurse from Rennes cured of intestinal tuberculosis, a naval officer from Toulon whose stubborn fistula closed, and a boy, blind and paralysed at three, who recovered sight and movement. The second, 'Pèlerinage', follows a pilgrim's whole day: Mass, prayer at the grotto, the sick immersed in the baths, the rosary, the procession of the Blessed Sacrament and the candlelit night procession. The third, 'Imprévus', is the most striking. Rouquier's camera had filmed two sick women hours or days before they were cured, and he shows them again afterwards.
inclusion: Rouquier made his name with Farrebique (1946), a year in the life of a peasant family in the Rouergue, and he brings the same patience to Lourdes. The film was commissioned, and it could easily have been an apologetic tract. Jean Collet, writing on Rouquier for the Encyclopædia Universalis, judges it instead the most honest and most moving record of what happens at Lourdes during the pilgrimages, and perhaps the finest and least known of Rouquier's films. Its strength is its method: it lets the Medical Bureau's files, the pilgrims and the sick speak, and it does not hide the souvenir trade. The young Jacques Demy was Rouquier's assistant. It is rarely shown and hard to find.
themes: The film's subject is the shrine as a place of prayer and of cures, and it treats both seriously. The Medical Bureau's procedure, by which doctors examine a cure before the Church is asked to judge it, is shown in detail. The second part records the devotions that fill a Lourdes day: Mass, the rosary, the baths, the blessing of the sick and the eucharistic procession. Rouquier's narration does not overstate. He presents the cures as facts the doctors could not explain and leaves the viewer to weigh them, which is close to the Church's own caution about Lourdes.
history: The apparitions to Bernadette Soubirous took place at the grotto of Massabielle in 1858. The Bureau des constatations médicales examines reported cures and selects those that appear both real and medically inexplicable before any bishop is asked to rule on them. Rouquier's film was produced by Les Productions du Parvis and opened in France on 9 November 1955; in the United States it was distributed by Brandon Films.
advisories:
Sick and disabled people are shown in their illness; nothing graphic.

Suitable for all ages, though younger children may find it slow.

title: Paul, Apostle of Christ
decision: PUBLISH: Richard Roeper's independent Chicago Sun-Times review (3/4, a 'thoughtful and faithful' telling) and Steven Greydanus's detailed review (B+, used for content only) establish a reverent, Scripture-based account of St Paul's last days and martyrdom that rejects violence against persecutors. The English subtitle file confirms the theology stays scriptural (grace in Pauline words, 2 Timothy read at the end) with no 'faith alone' framing, and that nothing presents the post-conciliar Church. St Peter is named only twice in passing, and no Eucharist or breaking of bread is spoken of; both omissions are disclosed.
summary: Andrew Hyatt's chamber drama of St Paul's last weeks in Nero's Mamertine prison, where St Luke visits him to record his memories while Rome's Christians face persecution.
synopsis: After the fire of Rome, Nero blames the Christians and has them burned as torches and thrown to beasts. Paul, old and worn, waits in the Mamertine prison under sentence of death. Luke slips into the city and gets into the cell, where he persuades Paul to recount his life so that it can be written down. Paul is haunted by the Christians he persecuted as Saul, and remembers his conversion and his baptism at the hands of Ananias. Outside, Priscilla and Aquila shelter the community, whose younger men want to fight back, and a failed rescue lands Luke in prison too. The prefect Mauritius, whose daughter is dying, turns in desperation to Luke, a physician. Luke heals the girl while Christians die in the circus. The community leaves Rome carrying Luke's writings, and Paul is beheaded.
inclusion: This is a small, talky film rather than the epic some expected, and it is better for it. James Faulkner gives the strongest performance as a worn, combative Paul, and Richard Roeper singles him out; Jim Caviezel's Luke is quiet and steady. Steven Greydanus calls the screenplay intelligent and thoughtful, and finds Paul's remorse over the Christians he persecuted the film's most effective thread. The story turns on a real question for a persecuted Church: whether to answer Nero with force. The film says no, and argues the point rather than assuming it. Malta stands in for a half-burned Rome, and the look is convincing for a $5 million production. The weaknesses are real. Some scenes play like a stage dialogue, a few lines sound too modern, and Greydanus finds the timeline of the closing scene confusing.
themes: The subject is Christian witness under persecution. Paul insists that love, not vengeance, is the answer to Nero, and the young men who want to free him by force are shown to be wrong. His guilt over his years as a persecutor gives the theme of forgiveness real weight: his sins, he says, were washed away by God's grace. Luke's healing of the prefect's daughter is presented as a miracle and as charity to an enemy, and Paul's death is martyrdom accepted. The language is Pauline and scriptural, with no 'faith alone' slogan. What is missing is the Church's structure: no Eucharist, no clergy, and St Peter named only in passing. Greydanus calls the absence of Peter, Linus and Clement an odd missed opportunity.
history: Tradition holds that St Paul was beheaded in Rome under Nero, and the Second Letter to Timothy, written from his last imprisonment, says that only Luke was with him. Tacitus records that Nero blamed the Christians for the fire of AD 64 and put many to death in cruel spectacles, some burned as torches. Priscilla and Aquila were tentmakers and co-workers of Paul named in Acts and in his letters.
liberties: Scripture places Luke with Paul in his last imprisonment, but the scheme of secretly taking down his memories, the prefect Mauritius and his daughter, and the armed faction among the Christians are invented. St Peter, traditionally martyred in the same persecution, does not appear and is mentioned only twice, as part of Paul's past. Greydanus notes that the story tracing the term 'Roman candle' to burning Christians is a late folk etymology.
advisories:
Bloody images of persecution: Christians burned alive as torches, burned bodies, and martyrs sent to the beasts in the circus.

Paul's beheading; a failed armed rescue.

Rated PG-13 in the United States; Greydanus suggests teens and up.

The Roman church is shown without the Mass or its clergy, and St Peter is only mentioned.
