title: Quo Vadis?
decision: PUBLISH: Maria Wyke's scholarly study documents a faithful set of 'moving illustrations' of Sienkiewicz's Catholic novel: Peter preaching in the catacomb, Christ appearing to Peter on the Via Appia, Paul baptising the repentant Chilo, the martyrs in the arena, and a closing vision of Christ breaking the chains of the faithful. Giovanni Lasi's Cinema Ritrovato note confirms identity, the 2026 restoration and the film's standing. Cines, the producer, was funded by the Vatican's bank; the film's sympathies are plainly with the Church.
summary: Guazzoni's 1913 Cines spectacle of Sienkiewicz's novel, with Peter in the catacombs, the burning of Rome and the arena martyrs, was the first great epic of cinema.
synopsis: In Nero's Rome the patrician officer Vinicius falls for Lygia, a Christian hostage guarded by the giant Ursus. Following her with the informer Chilo, he comes to a night gathering of Christians outside the city, where the apostle Peter preaches to them. His pride gives way as he comes to respect Lygia's faith. Nero burns Rome and blames the Christians, and a persecution follows; the faithful are condemned to the Circus and die among the lions. Lygia is tied to the back of a bull and Ursus saves her by breaking its neck. Peter, leaving the city, meets Christ on the Appian Way and turns back to Rome to die. The penitent Chilo is baptised by Paul. Nero, abandoned, dies, and the film ends with a vision of Christ freeing the faithful from their chains.
inclusion: Quo Vadis? ran for two hours with thousands of extras and huge built sets, and it changed what audiences expected from a film. It opened at the Astor in New York, where it ran for nine months, and King George V saw it at the Royal Albert Hall. Giovanni Lasi credits Guazzoni, a trained painter, with a new sense of depth and spectacle: crowds arranged in great masses, strong contrasts of light and silhouette, real Roman locations for the Appian Way and the Borghese gardens. Wyke shows how scenes quote Gérôme's paintings of the Christian martyrs. The acting and the tableau construction are of their time, and the French critic René Doumic found the whole thing stupefying. Its importance in film history is beyond dispute, and its story is the Church's.
themes: Sienkiewicz wrote a Catholic novel, ending at Peter's basilica on the Vatican hill, and Wyke reads the film as an Italian Catholic allegory: the persecuted early Christians stand for Catholics under a hostile secular state. Peter is shown preaching in the catacomb, his presence in Rome given the weight of archaeology, and the Quo vadis, Domine? meeting on the Appian Way, where Christ turns Peter back towards martyrdom, is filmed on the real road. Conversion runs through the story: Vinicius is won by Lygia's purity, and Chilo the betrayer is forgiven and baptised by Paul. The film adds a final vision of Christ breaking the chains of kneeling believers.
history: Christians were executed in Rome after the fire of AD 64, as Tacitus records. Catholic tradition holds that Peter and Paul were martyred in Rome under Nero, and the Quo vadis story comes from the apocryphal Acts of Peter. Lygia, Vinicius, Ursus and Chilo are Sienkiewicz's inventions. His novel appeared in 1896 and won him wide fame before his Nobel Prize in 1905.
liberties: The film follows the novel's main line but compresses it into a sequence of illustrated episodes linked by long titles. Its last shot, Christ breaking the chains of the faithful, has no source in the novel. Lasi's note dates it 1912/13; it premiered in Berlin in March 1913.
advisories:
Arena violence: Christians thrown to lions, a gladiator fight, a woman bound to a bull.

The burning of Rome and scenes of Nero's court and banquets.

Silent, with long explanatory titles; older children and up.

title: Quo Vadis
decision: GREY: Identity and fidelity are established (Wikipedia, Kino Muranów, Ewa Skwara in Classica, Marek Zieleniewski in Wprost, Jonathan Rosenbaum). The English subtitle file narrows the coda question: the last dialogue is the Quo vadis scene, Peter turning back to Rome (02:10:18–02:10:52), and nothing is spoken between it and the end titles (02:11:06). The present-day coda is therefore wordless and brief, a passing modern image rather than the film's interpretive voice, so rule (b) does not apply. It stays GREY for the nudity at Nero's feasts and because what the closing images show of modern Rome is still undescribed.
summary: Jerzy Kawalerowicz's lavish, faithful Polish adaptation of Sienkiewicz's novel of Nero's persecution, with Franciszek Pieczka as St Peter and an added ending in modern Rome.
synopsis: In Nero's Rome the young patrician Marcus Vinicius falls for Lygia, a Christian hostage of barbarian birth raised in the house of Aulus Plautius and Pomponia Graecina. His uncle Petronius, Nero's arbiter of taste, contrives to have her handed over to Vinicius, but she escapes with her giant protector Ursus and hides among the Christians. Vinicius tracks her down with the wrestler Croton; Ursus kills Croton and Vinicius is wounded. Nursed by the Christians he came to rob, he is converted and baptised. When Rome burns, Nero blames the Christians and sends them to die in the arena. Lygia is bound to the back of a bull, and Ursus wrestles it down; Nero spares them. Peter, urged to flee, meets Christ on the Appian Way and turns back to Rome. A brief wordless coda shows him in the Rome of today.
inclusion: This is the most faithful screen version of Sienkiewicz's novel, made by one of Poland's most respected directors as his last film. Kawalerowicz said repeatedly that he wanted to follow the book and its moral message; Ewa Skwara's study finds that the result looks like the nineteenth century's idea of Rome, closer to Alma-Tadema's paintings than to modern scholarship, and that Polish audiences loved it. It was the most popular Polish film of its year, with 4.2 million admissions. Critics were cooler. Marek Zieleniewski in Wprost praised Jerzy Trela's Chilon, Michał Bajor's Nero and Bogusław Linda's restrained Petronius, but found the film static and stagey and the romance rushed. Jonathan Rosenbaum thought it stacks up well against the 1951 MGM version, though he preferred Ustinov's Nero.
themes: The novel's Christian substance is the conversion of a pagan through charity and the witness of the martyrs, and the film keeps it. Vinicius is won less by argument than by the Christians who nurse the man who came to seize Lygia, and he is baptised in the name of the Trinity; so, at the last, is the informer Chilon. The persecution after the fire is presented as martyrdom. St Peter, played by Franciszek Pieczka, is the apostle of the Roman Christians, as in the book. The last spoken scene is the legend that gives the story its title: Peter meets Christ on the road, asks where He is going, and turns back to Rome. Kawalerowicz's added coda in modern Rome is wordless.
history: Tacitus records that Nero blamed the Christians for the great fire of AD 64 and had many put to death in cruel spectacles. Tradition places the martyrdom of St Peter in the same persecution. Sienkiewicz published Quo Vadis in 1895–96 after close study of Tacitus and other Roman writers; its title comes from the legend of Peter meeting Christ on the Appian Way as he fled Rome.
liberties: Kawalerowicz follows the novel closely, compressing its many strands. His main addition is a brief, wordless closing image that brings St Peter into present-day Rome. Zieleniewski found the romance rushed, and the arena deaths, in the version he saw, oddly bloodless.
advisories:

It is wordless and says nothing about the present-day Church; a description of what it shows would settle whether it is more than a visual flourish.

title: Saint Joan
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (St Joan of Arc) but built on Shaw's thesis that Joan was a Protestant and a nationalist before her time (Shaw's Preface and Scene IV, per Gale's Drama for Students). Legion of Decency A-II. Not REJECT because the thesis is argued rather than preached, the churchmen are given serious speeches and Greene's adaptation softens Shaw by blaming individual judges; not PUBLISH because the film's framing of Joan's sanctity against Church authority is a real doctrinal question.
summary: Preminger's film of Shaw's play, adapted by Graham Greene, with eighteen-year-old Jean Seberg as Joan: intelligent talk, a miscast lead and Shaw's argument with the Church.
synopsis: In 1456, after Joan's sentence has been annulled, the ageing Charles VII dreams that she visits him, and the story unfolds in flashback. A farm girl who hears the voices of saints persuades a local captain, then the feeble Dauphin, to let her lead the army. She raises the siege of Orléans and sees Charles crowned at Reims. Then the court and the generals tire of her. Captured and sold to the English, she is tried at Rouen by Bishop Cauchon and the Inquisitor, while the Earl of Warwick wants her burned whatever the verdict. Frightened, she signs a recantation; when she learns that she will be imprisoned for life, she tears it up and goes to the stake. The film returns to Charles, waking from his dream.
inclusion: This is the most serious screen version of Shaw's play, with a fine supporting cast: John Gielgud as Warwick, Anton Walbrook as Cauchon, Felix Aylmer as the Inquisitor. Graham Greene cut a play of three and a half hours to under two, and the pressbook claimed nearly all the dialogue was still Shaw's. The trial scenes, where Shaw gives the churchmen real arguments, are the strongest part. Much of the rest was poorly received. Preminger chose Seberg from thousands of applicants, and critics found her out of her depth; the London Times faulted a scrappy, rearranged first half; Dennis Schwartz grades it C-minus. Preminger later blamed himself, saying he had treated the play as an intellectual debate about religion instead of a legend.
themes: Shaw admired Joan but built his play on a thesis. His Preface calls her a Protestant martyr and an early apostle of nationalism, as well as a pious Catholic, and in the tent scene Cauchon and Warwick name the threat she poses: private judgment set against the Church. Shaw's churchmen are not villains; Cauchon is sincere and the Inquisitor reasoned. That fairness carries the problem with it, because Joan's sanctity becomes the triumph of the individual conscience over the Church's authority. Greene, a Catholic, shifted the blame from the whole Church to individual judges. Her voices are presented as real to her and left unexplained.
history: Joan of Arc was burned at Rouen in 1431. A papal commission annulled her sentence in 1456. She was beatified in 1909 and canonised in 1920, and Shaw wrote Saint Joan in 1923. Preminger paid Shaw's estate $100,000 for the rights. Shaw had written his own screen version in the 1930s, which Preminger and Greene said they did not know. The film premiered at the Paris Opéra in May 1957.
liberties: The film opens with Shaw's epilogue as a dream of Charles VII and returns to it, rather than ending there. Shaw's anachronisms remain, with talk of Protestantism and nationalism a century before either existed. The film makes no mention of Joan's beatification or canonisation. The trial is heavily compressed.
advisories:
Joan's burning is shown, briefly.

Battle scenes are short and not graphic.

Suitable for teenagers and adults. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

Shaw's reading of Joan as a champion of private judgment against the Church runs through the dialogue.

grey.question: Shaw's Joan is a great woman, but his play presents her as a forerunner of Protestantism and nationalism, a private conscience defying the Church, and the film keeps much of that argument. The churchmen are given fair speeches, yet the drama turns Joan's sanctity into a victory of the individual over ecclesiastical authority, which is not why the Church canonised her. Greene's script softens this by blaming individual judges rather than the Church. Viewers who know the history, and the Church's own verdict on Joan in 1456 and 1920, can weigh Shaw's case.

title: Saint Joan the Maid
originalTitle: La Merveilleuse Vie de Jeanne d'Arc
alternateTitles: La Merveilleuse Vie de Jeanne d'Arc, fille de Lorraine

decision: GREY: Identity is secure (Silent Era; Wikipedia citing Nowell-Smith; Internet Archive copy) and the film's course is known: Joan's life from the first visions at Domrémy in 1428 to her burning at Rouen, made for the fifth centenary of her death after her 1920 canonisation, with Simone Genevois praised for her fervour and purity (BAMPFA 1987 note; Girls with Guns review). No source assesses how it treats her voices, her faith or her judges. Not HOLD, because identity and content are clear. It would move to PUBLISH with a review that addresses the religious content, a 1929 Catholic press notice (La Croix, Centrale Catholique), or a reading of the French intertitles of the Internet Archive copy.
summary: Marco de Gastyne's two-hour French epic of St Joan, shot at Carcassonne, Chinon and Mont-Saint-Michel, with seventeen-year-old Simone Genevois as the Maid.
synopsis: The film follows Joan from 1428, when the shepherd girl first hears her voices at Domrémy, to her death at Rouen in 1431. She goes to the Dauphin Charles (Jean Debucourt) at Chinon, is given command alongside captains such as La Hire and Gilles de Rais, and leads the relief of Orléans, including the assault on the Tourelles. Later she is captured, and at Rouen she is tried by a church court in which the informer Nicolas Loiseleur plays his part. The trial ends in her condemnation. She walks to the stake and is burned, and the film stops abruptly at her death.
inclusion: Gastyne's film was made in 1927–28, in the same years as Dreyer's Passion of Joan of Arc, and was buried by its reputation. The two are opposites: Dreyer confines himself to the trial and the faces; Gastyne gives the whole life, with real castles and towns as settings and thousands of extras for the siege of Orléans, filmed at Carcassonne, and the trial at Mont-Saint-Michel. A 1987 Pacific Film Archive note calls it the more commercial of the two and praises Genevois's youthful fervour, mysterious purity and very human terror. Jim McLennan of Girls with Guns found the trial slow but the battles and the walk to the stake powerful. The Cinémathèque française reconstructed it in the 1980s, and a copy is on the Internet Archive.
themes: The film's frame is Joan's sanctity: it was made for the 500th anniversary of her death, shortly after her canonisation in 1920, and its French title presents her life as marvellous. It begins with her visions and treats her mission as a call from God that she obeys. Reviewers stress her purity and courage rather than any modern psychological reading. How the voices are shown, how the church court is portrayed and whether Joan's faith is stressed at the stake have not been described by any source found.

grey.question: This French epic tells the life of St Joan from her first visions to her burning, and reviewers praise Simone Genevois's purity and fervour. What is missing is any account of how the film treats the faith itself: how her voices are shown, how the church court and Bishop Cauchon are portrayed, and what is said at the stake. A review addressing these points, a 1929 French Catholic press notice, or a reading of the French intertitles would settle it.

history: Joan of Arc (c. 1412–1431) heard her voices at Domrémy, raised the siege of Orléans in 1429 and saw Charles VII crowned at Reims. She was captured in 1430, tried for heresy at Rouen under Bishop Pierre Cauchon and burned on 30 May 1431. She was rehabilitated in 1456, beatified in 1909 and canonised in 1920.

title: Under the Sun of Satan
decision: GREY: Identity is secure (Cannes festival record, KVIFF archive, Wikipedia). Independent reviews (Harvard Film Archive, Reeling Reviews, Movies That Make You Think) establish a close adaptation of Bernanos centred on a priest, penance, confession and a personal Devil, and also its open questions: the film leaves the source of Donissan's gifts ambiguous, Mouchette kills herself after his intervention, and the director was an avowed atheist. These are reservations a reader can weigh, not a heterodox thesis. A scene-level French study comparing the dead-child episode with the novel would settle whether Pialat's ambiguity is Bernanos's own (then PUBLISH) or his addition.

grey.question: Pialat follows Bernanos closely: a real, personal Devil, a priest of heroic penance and a battle for a sinner's soul. But the film, made by an avowed atheist, leaves open whether Donissan's power to read souls, and his attempt to raise a dead child, come from God or from Satan's flattery of his pride. A young woman kills herself after he confronts her, and he carries her body into the church. Viewers who know the novel will read it as a Catholic tragedy; others may take it as a study of religious obsession.

summary: Pialat's harsh, Palme d'Or-winning version of Bernanos's first novel: a clumsy, self-scourging country priest meets Satan on a night road and fights for a murderess's soul.
synopsis: Donissan, a young priest of peasant stock, is a poor preacher and an awkward curate under the shrewd, experienced Menou-Segrais, and he punishes himself with a hair shirt and the discipline. Mouchette, a sixteen-year-old in the district, shoots her lover, the Marquis de Cadignan, and his death passes for suicide. Pregnant, she turns to another lover, Dr Gallet, who refuses to help her end the pregnancy. Walking at night to a distant parish, Donissan falls in with a friendly horse-dealer who is Satan; afterwards he finds he can see into souls. He meets Mouchette and urges her to repent. Soon after, she kills herself, and Donissan carries her body into the church, a scandal that gets him sent away. Years later, a priest with a reputation for holiness, he prays over a dead child, whose eyes open. He dies alone in his confessional.
inclusion: Pialat, a professed unbeliever, made one of the most physical films about a priest. Gérard Depardieu's Donissan is a big, clumsy man who scourges himself, walks for miles and cannot preach, and the Harvard Film Archive singles out the vulnerability Depardieu finds in him. Sandrine Bonnaire's Mouchette is fierce and scornful of God. The photography of the Pas-de-Calais is cold and grey, and the supernatural, as the HFA notice puts it, surfaces inside an ordinary realism: the Devil is simply a talkative man on a dark road. The film is also elliptical, hard to follow without the novel, and at times stagey. It was booed at Cannes and won the Palme d'Or unanimously. Pialat said he had, if anything, been too faithful to Bernanos, and the film keeps the novel's core: a war for souls fought by a man who doubts himself.
themes: This is Bernanos's Catholicism at its darkest. Satan is real, personal and patient, and holiness is a combat. Donissan's penances, his gift of reading souls, his long hours in the confessional and his sense of being a mere zero beside other numbers all come from the novel. So does the ambiguity, and that is the difficulty. The film never settles whether his gift comes from God or from the Devil who has marked him, and his prayer over the dead child can be read as spiritual pride. Mouchette's suicide follows his intervention. Some reviewers, quoting Richard Brody, read the whole as a nonbeliever's study of religion's psychological power; the Catholic reading is equally open.
history: Georges Bernanos published Sous le soleil de Satan, his first novel, in 1926. Pialat and Sylvie Danton adapted it, and filming began on 20 October 1986 in Fressin and Montreuil-sur-Mer, Pas-de-Calais. It premiered in competition at Cannes on 14 May 1987 and won the Palme d'Or by a unanimous jury, the first French winner in 21 years. It opened in France on 2 September 1987 and drew about 816,000 admissions.

title: The 26 Martyrs of Japan
decision: PUBLISH: Goffredo Fofi's review (Il Sole 24 Ore, 2017, summarised in the Cinema Ritrovato note) is an independent, substantive treatment: he praises the film's skill and its respectful view from inside Japanese culture and its Christian community, and contrasts its decency with later propaganda. The film depicts the 1597 Nagasaki martyrdom faithfully in four chapters ending with the crucifixions. The martyrs were beatified in 1627 and canonised in 1862, so no hard rule applies. Made with Catholic help and co-written by a Jesuit, Fr Hermann Heuvers; Japanese Catholic hierarchy received it well (contemporary Catholic press cited by Wikipedia).
summary: A Nikkatsu silent epic, made by Japanese Catholics in 1931, of the Franciscans, Jesuits and Japanese tertiaries crucified at Nagasaki in 1597.
synopsis: The Spanish Franciscan Pedro Bautista preaches in the Kyoto region, where a Christian community grows among ordinary Japanese, many of them members of the Franciscan Third Order. When a Spanish ship, the San Felipe, is wrecked on the coast, suspicion grows that the missionaries are the vanguard of conquest, and the ruler Toyotomi Hideyoshi orders a persecution. Missionaries and laymen are arrested, among them a child and a converted thief who becomes the first victim. The film, told in four chapters that follow the phases of the mission, ends on a beach at Nagasaki, where the twenty-six are crucified and run through with lances. An epilogue recalls their canonisation at the Vatican in 1862.
inclusion: This is a rare thing: a major Japanese studio film about the Japanese martyrs, made in the last years of silent cinema by people who shared their faith. Seiju Hirayama, a Catholic landowner, put much of his fortune into it, and the Jesuit Hermann Heuvers co-wrote the script. Goffredo Fofi, reviewing the 2017 restoration, praises Ikeda's command of late silent technique, the way the drama and documentary-style passages support each other, and the respect with which it shows Japanese life from inside its Christian community. He faults it for not exploring the political motives behind the persecution. The surviving version, found among Salesian holdings and restored in 4K in Turin, runs about 65 minutes of an original two and a half hours.
themes: The film is about martyrdom as witness. The victims include European friars and Jesuits, but most are Japanese lay tertiaries, and a child among them is given particular attention, so the faith is shown as fully Japanese, not foreign. A thief converted by the missionaries is the first to die. The ending reproduces the crucifixion at Nagasaki, deliberately echoing Calvary, and the film closes with the Church's recognition of their sanctity. Fofi notes the film's decency and restraint. Its makers intended it partly as a defence of Japanese Catholics, honoured by Rome, against suspicion at home.
history: On 5 February 1597, on Hideyoshi's orders, twenty-six Christians were crucified on Nishizaka hill at Nagasaki: six Franciscans, among them Pedro Bautista, three Japanese Jesuits, including Paul Miki, and seventeen Japanese laymen, several of them boys. They were beatified in 1627 and canonised by Pius IX in 1862.
liberties: Only about 65 minutes survive of a film originally around 150 minutes long, so the restored version compresses the story. The film's account of the San Felipe affair and Hideyoshi's motives is simplified, as Fofi notes. The converted thief's role reflects the film's dramatisation rather than any established detail of the martyrs' lives.
advisories:
The crucifixion of the martyrs, with lances; the death of a child.

Scenes of arrest and persecution.

Silent, Japanese intertitles (the restoration is subtitled); suitable for older children with guidance.

title: The Cardinal
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a priest's vocation; Church teaching on mixed marriage and on the unborn child). Legion of Decency A-III (Motion Picture Exhibitor Legion tables, 1963–64); contemporary reviews (Exhibitor; James Daane in Christianity Today; Crowther and Crist via TCM and Varden). The English subtitle file shows the closing speech is anti-totalitarian Americanism ('That is America's creed. That is the Gospel of the Church') ending in a prayer 'for the liberty and exaltation of our church', not a case for conciliar religious liberty; the Vienna section defends the Church's rights over family and schools against the Nazis; the Georgia section is about a segregated Catholic school and a church burned by the Klan, with no interracial marriage. The one line to state is the hero's unqualified answer to a parish class that anyone following conscience can reach heaven. Not REJECT: the film's thesis is not the post-conciliar programme. Joseph Ratzinger's role as Vatican liaison is a fact only.
summary: Preminger's three-hour saga of an Irish-American priest's rise from Boston curate to cardinal, through family tragedy, the Klan and the Anschluss: sincere, handsome and uneven.
synopsis: In 1939 Stephen Fermoyle is created a cardinal in Rome, and his life returns in flashback. Newly ordained in 1917, he comes home to Boston, where his sister Mona wants to marry a Jewish man who will not promise to raise their children Catholic. Stephen advises her to give him up, and she leaves home and goes astray. Sent to a poor country parish under the dying Father Halley, he learns humility. When Mona, pregnant out of wedlock, is in a fatal labour, the doctor says only killing the child can save her; Stephen refuses, and she dies. Shaken, he takes leave in Vienna, where a young woman, Annemarie, falls in love with him; he keeps his vows. Back in service, he confronts the Klan in Georgia, becomes a bishop and confronts Cardinal Innitzer over the Nazis.
inclusion: It is one of the few big Hollywood films to take a priest's whole career seriously, and it was shot on real locations, including Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome and St Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna. John Huston as the shrewd Cardinal Glennon and Burgess Meredith as the dying country priest are excellent; the film earned six Oscar nominations and won the Golden Globe for best drama. Tom Tryon is the weak point. Bosley Crowther called his priest a callow cliché, and Judith Crist found the whole a mélange of melodrama and mouthed pieties, while Motion Picture Exhibitor called it provocative and dignified. Bishop Erik Varden, watching it sixty years later, is struck that a mainstream film could show the Church as a source of moral authority.
themes: The film takes Catholic teaching seriously enough to dramatise its cost. Stephen tells his sister plainly what a mixed marriage requires and that a civil wedding would be no marriage, and in the childbirth scene he refuses to let her child be killed to save her. He takes leave from the priesthood but keeps his vows. Two things trouble. He tells a parish class that anyone who does God's will according to conscience can reach heaven, and a boy's 'Then what's the use of being Catholic?' goes unanswered. And the closing speech calls 'life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness' both America's creed and the Gospel of the Church, the confusion Leo XIII warned against in 1899, though it ends with a prayer for the liberty and exaltation of the Church.
history: Henry Morton Robinson's 1950 best-seller drew loosely on the career of Francis Spellman, Archbishop of New York, whose pressure kept it off the screen for years. Cardinal Theodor Innitzer of Vienna did welcome the Anschluss in 1938. The Vatican liaison for the European shoot was the young Joseph Ratzinger. The film opened in Boston in December 1963, during the Second Vatican Council.
liberties: Fermoyle is fictional. The Vienna episode built around Innitzer and the Nazis was Preminger's most significant addition to the novel. The Georgia episode with the Klan and a Black priest is freely dramatised.
advisories:
A woman's death in childbirth after a refusal to kill the child; the dilemma is explicit.

A young woman's promiscuity and an out-of-wedlock pregnancy, implied rather than shown.

A priest is beaten by the Klan; a suicide; Nazi violence.

For adults and older teenagers. The Legion of Decency rated it A-III.

A loose statement on the salvation of non-Catholics goes unqualified, and the closing speech equates American liberty with the Gospel.

grey.question: The Cardinal upholds Catholic teaching at its hardest points: its hero refuses to let his sister's unborn child be killed, and keeps his vows when a woman falls in love with him. But it presents those rules as costly and doubtful and the Church as rigid. The hero tells children that anyone who follows his conscience can be saved, without the qualifications the Church attached, and the film ends on a speech calling the American creed the Gospel of the Church. The Legion of Decency rated it for adults. Viewers can admire its seriousness while asking whose side it is really on.

title: The Greatest Story Ever Told
decision: GREY: AFI (identity, production) and Steven Greydanus (B+, +3, a substantive review) establish a reverent, Christ-centred film released in February 1965, before the Council closed; its non-denominational production does not put it out of scope because Christ, the Eucharist and the Resurrection are central and nothing contradicts Catholic teaching outright. The reservation is the Gospel revisionism Greydanus flags: Judas half-excused and given an invented death, Lazarus merged with the rich young man. This is a milder form of the Judas problem in Jesus of Nazareth, without that film's Nostra Aetate framing. A contemporary Legion of Decency classification without note would move it to PUBLISH; if the editor treats the Judas change as the same fault as Zeffirelli's, REJECT.

grey.question: Stevens's film is reverent, and it plainly presents Christ as the divine Word who works real miracles, institutes the Eucharist, dies, rises and ascends. Its departures from the Gospels are the issue. Judas becomes a half-sympathetic figure and dies by walking into a Temple fire rather than by hanging; Lazarus is merged with the rich young man; Satan appears as an invented hermit. Greydanus counts the Judas change the most damaging. Viewers who know the Gospel text will notice and can correct these changes; younger viewers should be told.

summary: George Stevens's slow, reverent, star-crowded Life of Christ, from the Nativity to the Ascension, with Max von Sydow as a grave and sovereign Jesus.
synopsis: The Magi follow the star to Bethlehem; Herod the Great orders the massacre of the infants, and the Holy Family flees to Egypt. Years later John the Baptist preaches at the Jordan and baptises Jesus, who goes into the wilderness and is tempted by a sinister hermit. Jesus calls the Twelve, teaches, heals and raises Lazarus, which alarms Caiaphas and Herod Antipas. He enters Jerusalem and eats the Last Supper with His disciples, instituting the Eucharist and foretelling Judas's betrayal and Peter's denials. Judas hands Him over in Gethsemane for thirty pieces of silver. He is tried before the Sanhedrin, Pilate and Herod, scourged and crucified, with Simon of Cyrene carrying His cross. Judas throws himself into a Temple fire. Jesus rises, appears to Mary Magdalene and the disciples, convinces Thomas, and sends them out to all nations.
inclusion: Stevens spent years on the film, and it shows both ways. The images are its strength: shot in the American Southwest, the canyons stand in for an empty, monumental Holy Land, and many compositions look like devotional paintings. Alfred Newman's score is lush, and the raising of Lazarus, cut to Handel's Hallelujah Chorus, is the sequence Greydanus rates highest. Max von Sydow plays Christ as the sovereign Lord of St John's Gospel; Greydanus finds him persuasively authoritative, if not warm. The faults are well known. The pace is stately to the point of torpor, the star cameos distract, and Charlton Heston's Baptist is overblown. Time called it impeccable boredom; Greydanus still ranks it above most Hollywood Bible epics for its prayerful spirit. Watch a long version: the 1967 general release lost more than an hour.
themes: Christ's divinity is never in doubt. The film opens on the prologue of St John and presents Him as the eternal Word, who forgives sins, works real miracles, institutes the Eucharist at the Last Supper, dies, rises and gives the Great Commission. Dorothy McGuire's Mary is quiet and reverent. The problems lie in the details. Judas is made an almost sympathetic figure, and his death is changed from the Gospel's hanging to a leap into the Temple fire; Greydanus calls this the departure that hurts most. Lazarus is merged with the rich young man. Satan becomes a shadowy hermit. Beyond what the Gospels give, there is nothing distinctly Catholic, and nothing anti-Catholic either.
history: Twentieth Century-Fox bought Fulton Oursler's 1949 bestseller in 1954; Stevens took the project to United Artists, consulted dozens of Bible translations and sought the advice of Pope John XXIII. John E. Fitzgerald of Our Sunday Visitor advised on the script. David Lean and Jean Negulesco shot some sequences. The film cost nearly $20 million, opened in New York on 15 February 1965, received five Oscar nominations and lost money; the 1967 reissue was cut to about 141 minutes.
liberties: Judas dies by throwing himself into the Temple's sacrificial fire, not by hanging (Matthew 27:5). Lazarus is merged with the rich young man. Satan is an invented 'Dark Hermit'. The four Gospels are blended freely, the Holy Land is the American Southwest, and dialogue sometimes slips into flat modern idiom.
advisories:
The scourging and crucifixion are restrained; Greydanus calls the Passion restrained.

No sexual content or bad language.

Suitable for all ages, though the length (about 3 hours 20 minutes in the usual restored version) and pace will tax children.

Judas's motive and death are changed from the Gospel account.

title: The Hoodlum Priest
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a Jesuit's apostolate to ex-convicts; the good-thief theme). Strong pre-1965 Catholic recognition: the International Catholic Office for the Cinema award at Cannes 1961 (AFI); Cardinal Ritter attended the premiere (TCM). Reservations: the film argues against capital punishment, and the real Fr Clark repudiated it (TCM; Motion Picture Exhibitor reports the Globe-Democrat controversy). Legion rating not found (OCR gap). Would be PUBLISH if the Founder treats the anti-death-penalty thrust as a tolerable prudential view.
summary: Don Murray plays the real Jesuit Fr Charles Dismas Clark, who works with ex-convicts in St Louis and walks a young killer to the gas chamber.
synopsis: St Louis, around 1960. Fr Charles Clark, a Jesuit known on the streets as the Hoodlum Priest, works with delinquents and men out of prison, speaking their language and finding them work. He takes on Billy Lee Jackson, a young thief just released from the state penitentiary, clears him of a false charge and gets him a job at a produce market, where Billy falls for a girl from a wealthy family. With the help of a criminal lawyer, Louis Rosen, Clark raises money to open a halfway house for ex-convicts. Then Billy is fired for a theft he did not commit, and in a botched robbery he kills a man. Clark persuades him to surrender. Billy is sentenced to death, and before the gas chamber Clark tells him about Dismas, the good thief promised Paradise.
inclusion: It is a sober, unsentimental film about a working priest, made cheaply on real locations, including Dismas House and the Missouri State Penitentiary, and shot in hard black and white by Haskell Wexler. Don Murray, who produced and co-wrote it, plays Clark as tough and quick rather than saintly, and Keir Dullea, in his first film, is affecting as Billy. A. H. Weiler in the New York Times praised its authentic look and pace. It competed at Cannes in 1961, where it received the award of the International Catholic Office for the Cinema, and the National Board of Review named it one of the year's ten best. The second half becomes an argument against the death penalty, and the execution is long and harrowing.
themes: The film shows a priest's apostolate among the lost, and its Catholic substance is concrete: a Jesuit meeting criminals on their own ground, finding them work and a roof, and staying with them when they fail. The centre is the last night of Billy's life. Clark cannot save his life, so he works to save his soul, and the spiritual climax is the story of Dismas, the thief who repented on the cross and was promised Paradise. That is sound and moving. The film's other aim, to show the gas chamber as an atrocity, sits uneasily with the Church's traditional teaching, which upheld the State's right to put murderers to death.
history: Charles Dismas Clark (1901–63), a Jesuit of St Louis, took his nickname from the good thief and worked with prisoners and ex-convicts. In 1959 he opened Dismas House, the first halfway house of its kind. He at first welcomed the film, then sided with the St Louis Globe-Democrat, which attacked its accuracy after the premiere, and repudiated it. He died in August 1963.
liberties: Billy Lee Jackson and his story are fiction built around Clark's work. The St Louis Globe-Democrat disputed the film's truthfulness at its premiere, and Clark himself later repudiated it for reasons he did not make public.
advisories:
A killing in a robbery and a long, distressing execution in the gas chamber.

A criminal milieu, drinking and rough language for its period.

For teenagers and adults.

The film argues against the death penalty.

grey.question: The Hoodlum Priest is sound on what matters most: a Jesuit's care for criminals, and his effort to bring a condemned man to repentance through the example of the good thief. But it is also a case against capital punishment, built on a sympathetic young offender and a drawn-out gas-chamber scene, whereas the Church's traditional teaching upheld the State's right to execute murderers. The real Fr Clark repudiated the film after its premiere. Viewers can take its portrait of a priest while weighing its thesis.

title: The Life and Passion of Jesus Christ
originalTitle: La Vie et la passion de Jésus-Christ
decision: PUBLISH: Steven Greydanus's detailed review (A+, moral/spiritual +4, Kids & Up) establishes a reverent tableau Life of Christ from the Annunciation to the Ascension, drawing on Catholic tradition (Veronica's veil, St Michael in the flight to Egypt) with no doctrinal objection. Silent Era's independent DVD review confirms the surviving 44-minute Pathécolor print. Its place on the 1995 Vatican list is recorded as a fact only.
summary: Pathé's hand-coloured tableau Gospel, staged after Doré, runs from the Annunciation to the Ascension in short scenes that work like a moving set of holy pictures.
synopsis: The film is a chain of short scenes, each announced by a title card naming the event, as in a book of devotional pictures. It opens with the Annunciation and the Nativity, where shepherds and Magi gather at the manger, then follows the flight into Egypt, in which St Michael hides the Holy Family from Herod's soldiers. Episodes from the public life follow, among them a miraculous catch of fish combined with Christ walking on the water. The Passion follows, staged in the same pageant manner, including the way of the cross, where Veronica wipes Christ's face and finds his image on the cloth, and the Crucifixion. The film closes with the Resurrection and an Ascension in which Christ is seated at the Father's right hand, with the Holy Spirit, among saints and angels.
inclusion: This is one of the first long films ever made, built and rebuilt by Pathé between 1902 and 1905 until it ran about three-quarters of an hour, at a time when most films lasted a few minutes. The staging is frankly theatrical: painted backdrops, static camera, broad gestures. Greydanus argues that this stiffness works like the stylisation of an icon, and the Pathécolor stencil tinting, applied by hand to single objects in each frame, still gives some tableaux the look of coloured prints. It assumes the viewer knows the Gospel, since there are no dialogue titles. Greydanus found it among the most accessible Jesus films for small children. The surviving print, preserved by Haghefilm and Lobster Films, is clean and complete enough to be watched as a whole. It is a primitive film, but a coherent one.
themes: The film follows the shape of Catholic devotion rather than a single Gospel. It harmonises the evangelists and adds traditional material: Veronica's veil, the archangel guarding the Holy Family, and a Nativity in which Christ appears in the manger, an image Greydanus links to the patristic figure of light passing through glass. Mary is present throughout, from the Annunciation to Calvary. The ending insists on the Resurrection and Ascension rather than stopping at the tomb. Greydanus contrasts it with the more literal From the Manger to the Cross and prefers this pageant.
history: Pathé first released a Passion film in 1902 under Ferdinand Zecca and kept revising it; Wikipedia gives a May 1903 French release for the expanded version, while Greydanus dates the completed form to 1905, after Lucien Nonguet added the final scenes. Pathé made an entirely new version in 1907. Many tableaux follow Gustave Doré's Bible engravings.
advisories:
Mild, stylised depiction of the scourging and Crucifixion.

Silent, with title cards that name each scene but carry no dialogue; viewers need to know the Gospel story.

Suitable for children.

Dates and credits vary between sources because the film was revised several times between 1902 and 1905.

title: The Miracle of Father Malachia
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a monk's answered prayer and the world's response). Independent treatment from the Harvard Film Archive and the Zeughauskino programme (Ralf Schenk); Silver Bear for direction, Berlin 1961. Reservation: the satire extends to the hierarchy and to a religious order, and no pre-1965 Catholic rating (Film-Dienst, Legion) was found to judge its fairness. The Film-Dienst 1961 review or subtitles of the clergy scenes would settle it.
summary: Bernhard Wicki's satire from Bruce Marshall's novel: a simple monk's prayer removes a nightclub from beside his church, and the boom-town world turns the miracle into business.
synopsis: In a prosperous industrial town in the Ruhr, the Eden Bar, a dance club with a bad name, stands opposite a church. Father Malachias, a simple and unworldly monk, prays that it be taken away, and overnight the building and everyone in it vanish and reappear on a rocky island in the North Sea. Journalists, politicians and scientists look for explanations, and the Church is slow to call it a miracle. The empty plot becomes a fairground where traders sell holy water and souvenir models of the bar; a girl who was inside becomes a celebrity; investors build a casino on the island, which turns into a club for the rich. Dismayed by what his miracle has caused, Malachias prays again, and the Eden Bar returns to its old place.
inclusion: Wicki, fresh from The Bridge, made this as a broad satire of West Germany's economic miracle, plainly influenced by La Dolce Vita, and it won him the Silver Bear for direction at Berlin in 1961, along with German film awards. Introducing it at the Zeughauskino in 2012, Ralf Schenk described it as a dance round the golden calf in which nearly everyone takes part, from waitress to tycoon, and called it still strikingly relevant. The Harvard Film Archive notes how unusual it is among West German films in daring to show God acting. Horst Bollmann's Malachias is the one calm figure in a crowded, episodic and often frantic film, which ends in a long party sequence.
themes: The film takes its miracle seriously: Malachias's prayer is answered, and the world's response to a real sign is the target. Its Catholic heart is the monk's simple faith, which the film never mocks. The question is how it treats the Church itself. Accounts describe the hierarchy as reluctant to recognise the miracle for fear of losing control or being embarrassed, and the satire reaching the upper levels of a religious order. That could be fair comment on worldly churchmen or a jibe at the Church's proper caution about miracles, and the available sources do not settle which.
history: Bruce Marshall, a Scottish Catholic novelist, published Father Malachy's Miracle in the 1930s; sources give both 1931 and 1938. Wicki and Heinz Pauck moved the story to a West German industrial town of the economic-miracle years. The film premiered at the Berlin festival on 3 July 1961 and was West Germany's submission for the Academy Award.
advisories:
A nightclub and striptease milieu; sensuality is implied rather than explicit.

A long, wild party sequence.

For older teenagers and adults.

Churchmen are satirised along with everyone else.

Versions of 88, 122 and 126 minutes are recorded.

grey.question: The Miracle of Father Malachia believes in its miracle and loves its monk; its scorn is for a materialist society that can only sell what God has done. But the satire also reaches the Church: the hierarchy is shown as reluctant to admit the miracle for fear of losing face, and commentators speak of corruption reaching the upper levels of a religious order. No contemporary Catholic rating has been found. A viewing of the full version, or the German Catholic film review of 1961, would show whether the portrait of churchmen is fair satire or mockery.

title: The Nativity Story
decision: GREY: Identity (Danish Film Institute, Wikipedia) and content (Greydanus B+, used for content only; Jeffrey Overstreet in Christianity Today, independent of Catholic outlets) are established. The reservation is doctrinal: Mary is shown in labour pain (Fr John Zuhlsdorf; Br André Marie), contrary to the Roman Catechism's teaching that she gave birth without pain, and the specifically Marian texts are trimmed. Not REJECT because the film affirms the virginal conception and does not argue error as a thesis; the Founder may judge the birth scene grave enough to REJECT. The English subtitle file confirms the pain in dialogue: Joseph begs for shelter because 'my wife, she's in pain' (01:17:08), Mary calls out for him (01:17:27), and a cry is heard in the stable (01:19:37). It also shows that Mary does answer the angel 'Let it be done to me, according to your word' (00:21:43), so the earlier note that her answer is dropped is corrected.
summary: Catherine Hardwicke's sober, earthy telling of the Annunciation, Joseph's trial and the birth at Bethlehem, carried by Oscar Isaac's Joseph and marred by a labouring Mary.
synopsis: In Nazareth the teenage Mary is betrothed by her parents, Joachim and Anna, to the carpenter Joseph, a match she accepts without enthusiasm. The angel Gabriel tells her she will bear the Son of God, and she goes to her kinswoman Elizabeth, who is expecting John. Mary returns pregnant to a village that suspects the worst, and Joseph is in anguish until a dream tells him to take her as his wife. A census sends them on a hard journey to Bethlehem, while three Magi follow a star from the East and Herod grows uneasy. There is no room in Bethlehem, and Mary gives birth in a stable, where shepherds and the Magi come to worship. Warned in a dream, Joseph takes the family to Egypt before Herod's soldiers reach the town.
inclusion: Most screen Nativities are pageants. Hardwicke, working from Mike Rich's script, shot this one as rural life in first-century Palestine, with mud-brick villages, hard labour, Roman soldiers and Middle-Eastern accents; Steven Greydanus notes it may have the least Caucasian cast in the history of Hollywood Bible films. Its best asset is Oscar Isaac's Joseph, whom Jeffrey Overstreet in Christianity Today calls a detailed portrait of a virtuous man accepting enormous responsibility. Mychael Danna's score draws on 'O Come, O Come, Emmanuel'. The weaknesses are plain. Overstreet finds Keisha Castle-Hughes's Mary flat; the comic Magi jar; and the birth itself passes quickly in a stable that looks like a greeting card. A. O. Scott in the New York Times found an interesting film buried in the pageantry, while most critics were unimpressed. It held its world premiere in Vatican City.
themes: The film follows the Gospel infancy narratives closely, and Greydanus finds its faults mostly of omission. Gabriel greets Mary as 'favoured one' rather than 'full of grace'; she answers 'Let it be done to me according to your word', though not as the Lord's handmaid; the Magnificat is a short voice-over at the end. The virginal conception is plain: Mary has been with no man, and Joseph, having resolved not to accuse her, learns in a dream that the child is of the Holy Spirit. Her perpetual virginity is neither affirmed nor denied. The serious problem is the birth. Joseph begs for shelter because she is in pain, and she cries out in the stable, against the Roman Catechism's teaching that she gave birth without pain.
liberties: Mary is drawn as an ordinary, at first reluctant teenager, a characterisation meant to make her accessible to young viewers. Joseph is young. Elizabeth's labour and John's birth are shown. The Magi are played partly for comedy, and Herod's consultation with the scribes over Micah's prophecy is omitted.
advisories:
Two brief childbirth scenes, not graphic but intense: Elizabeth's and Mary's.

The massacre of the innocents is mostly implied; a Jewish girl is taken from her parents by Roman soldiers.

Rated PG in the United States; suitable for families.

Mary is shown giving birth in pain, contrary to traditional teaching.

grey.question: The Nativity Story is reverent and close to the Gospels, but it shows Our Lady in labour pain at Bethlehem: Joseph begs for shelter because she is in pain, and she cries out in the stable. The Roman Catechism teaches that she gave birth without pain, a virgin in giving birth as before and after, and traditional Catholic critics objected when the film opened. The script also thins out what is specifically Marian: no 'full of grace', no 'handmaid of the Lord', a shortened Magnificat. Viewers can weigh whether these are tolerable simplifications or a Protestant reading of Mary.

title: The Prisoner
decision: PUBLISH: Catholic-centred (a cardinal's faith under communist interrogation). Pre-1965 Catholic judgments are favourable: Grand Prize of the International Catholic Office for the Cinema 1956 (AFI, citing the NYT of 12 July 1956), commendation by Cardinal Griffin (Wikipedia), Legion of Decency A-II. Independent treatment from the Monthly Film Bulletin and NYT (via Wikipedia) and Roger Moore (2023). The open question about the cardinal's motives is disclosed.
summary: Alec Guinness plays a cardinal in a communist state whose interrogator breaks him not by torture but by turning his own humility against him.
synopsis: In an unnamed country of eastern Europe after the war, the government arrests its popular cardinal for treason. He resisted the Nazis and survived their torture, so his interrogator, a former comrade from the Resistance now loyal to the party, avoids physical violence. Forged evidence fails. Instead the interrogator uses sleeplessness, solitary confinement and the disruption of every routine, and searches the cardinal's past for a weakness. He finds it in his poor childhood, and in his fear that he became a priest out of vanity and a wish to escape it. Broken, the cardinal confesses at a show trial to everything he is charged with. His sentence is commuted so that he cannot become a martyr, and he walks out into a silent crowd. A subplot follows a young guard and a married woman.
inclusion: Guinness and Jack Hawkins have the film almost to themselves, and their duel is the reason to see it. The Monthly Film Bulletin praised Peter Glenville's first film and Guinness's soberly convincing cardinal, while finding the manner sometimes portentous; the New York Times called it grim and gripping. Its origin as a stage play shows. Roger Moore, reviewing it in 2023, found it stagebound and the guard's romance corny. In 1955 it was attacked from both sides: banned in Ireland as communist propaganda, dropped from Cannes and refused at Venice as anti-communist. The International Catholic Office for the Cinema gave it its Grand Prize for 1956, and Cardinal Griffin of Westminster commended it. Everyone saw the model: Mindszenty, and Stepinac.
themes: The film is about a priest's interior life under assault. The cardinal's strength is his faith, and the interrogator wins only by persuading him that his vocation was mixed with pride. The confession that follows is false, but it is also an act of self-abasement, and in the dock he seeks forgiveness from God, not from the court. He then accepts his survival, discredited, as a penance. The film leaves open how far his self-accusation is true; it never doubts the faith itself, and it is the interrogator who is left unsettled. Glenville insisted the film was not a tract for either side but the encounter of a man of God and a man of the State.
history: Cardinal József Mindszenty of Hungary was convicted at a show trial in 1949 after confessing under interrogation, and Archbishop Aloysius Stepinac of Zagreb had been convicted in 1946. Bridget Boland's play The Prisoner, drawing on both cases, was staged in 1954 with Guinness. The film opened in London in April 1955 and in New York in December, after a benefit preview at the Museum of Modern Art.
liberties: The cardinal and his country are fictional, a composite of the Mindszenty and Stepinac cases. The psychological method of the interrogation is the play's invention, not a reconstruction of either trial.
advisories:
Psychological cruelty: sleep deprivation, solitary confinement and humiliation; no torture is shown.

A subplot about a guard's love for a married woman; nothing explicit.

For teenagers and adults. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

The cardinal's false confession, and his doubts about his own motives, are central and partly left open.

title: The Robe
decision: PUBLISH: The National Legion of Decency classified the finished film A-I (morally unobjectionable for general patronage) and it received a Christopher Award, both pre-conciliar Catholic judgments recorded in the AFI Catalog; the Legion had warned against Lloyd C. Douglas's novel in 1948 (B), so the A-I marks a deliberate judgment on the film itself. Greydanus (B-, moral/spiritual +2, Kids & Up) establishes reverent content with Christ seen only from outside and St Peter as leader of the community, and is candid about its dramatic weakness. Christ, the Passion, Peter and martyrdom are central; nothing contrary to Catholic teaching is reported. Protestant authorship is disclosed.
summary: The first CinemaScope film follows the Roman tribune who crucified Christ and won His robe, through guilt and conversion under St Peter, to martyrdom under Caligula.
synopsis: Marcellus Gallio, a dissolute Roman tribune, is posted to Jerusalem after offending Caligula, taking with him the Greek slave Demetrius. He commands the detail that crucifies Jesus and wins the robe in a dice game at the foot of the cross. Demetrius, who has seen Christ on Palm Sunday, follows Him. Marcellus is tormented by guilt and fits of madness. The Emperor Tiberius sends him back to Palestine to find and destroy the robe and to spy on the Christians. In Cana he meets the followers of Jesus, among them Peter, comes to faith and joins them. Back in Rome he helps rescue Demetrius, who has been tortured, and Peter's prayer restores him. Caligula, now emperor, tries Marcellus for treason. He confesses Christ and walks to his death with Diana, who chooses to die with him.
inclusion: The Robe is best known as the film that launched CinemaScope, and it won Oscars for its sets and costumes. Leon Shamroy shot it in Technicolor and Alfred Newman wrote the score; it was nominated for Best Picture. As drama it is uneven. Greydanus singles out the Roman prologue and Demetrius's frantic search through Jerusalem on Holy Thursday night, and Peter's account of his denial and forgiveness, but finds Richard Burton stiff, the action scenes weak beside Ben-Hur, and the conversion more a matter of special effects than of a changed life. Bosley Crowther and Richard L. Coe were also unimpressed at the time. Its virtues are reverence and clarity, and Greydanus rates it suitable for children.
themes: Christ is never shown full-face: Demetrius is overwhelmed by a glance on Palm Sunday, and Calvary is seen through the soldiers who carry out the sentence. The robe is treated almost as a relic, an idea Greydanus finds intriguingly sacramental, though the film does not develop it. Peter, played as a gentle shepherd, recounts his triple denial and Christ's forgiveness, and leads the community that receives Marcellus. The ending is a confession of faith before the emperor and a martyrdom accepted freely. The film's Christianity is broad, from a Lutheran-trained novelist, but its subjects, the Passion, repentance and martyrdom, are wholly within Catholic tradition.
history: Lloyd C. Douglas's novel The Robe (1942) was one of the best-selling books of the 1940s. Producer Frank Ross bought the rights in 1942. The Legion of Decency gave the novel and proposed film a B rating in 1948, but classified the finished picture A-I in 1953. It premiered at the Roxy, New York, on 16 September 1953.
liberties: Marcellus, Diana, Demetrius and their story are fictional. Greydanus notes the film exaggerates the prominence of the early Church in Rome and invents a direct clash with Caligula, for which there is no historical basis. Peter is gentler than the Peter of the Gospels and Acts.
advisories:
Stylised action violence, a sword duel and the torture of a prisoner.

The Crucifixion is seen at a distance; mild Passion imagery.

Some veiled innuendo at Caligula's court.

Legion of Decency A-I; suitable for children.

title: The Shoes of the Fisherman
decision: REJECT: Rule (b) (Founder ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's exemplary pope is a figure of the conciliar aggiornamento: he befriends and defends a Teilhard-like theologian whose heterodoxy the film treats as a tragedy rather than an error (Greydanus: 'Teilhard de Chardin by way of Hans Küng'), prays a Jewish prayer at a deathbed as a model of dialogue, and at his coronation takes off the tiara and pledges the Church's wealth, to applause, as the climax. These gestures, modelled on the 1960s Church, are presented as the ideal of the papacy. Greydanus also flags 'muddled or misguided religious themes'. The conclave and coronation pageantry are pre-conciliar in form, which is why the case is close.

title: The Sign of the Cross
decision: REJECT: content, problem too grave. DeMille's Neronian martyr drama was itself one of the films that provoked the Catholic campaign which produced the Legion of Decency: a bishop cited it among Hollywood's 'vile and nauseating' films (OUP blog, Romanowski). The version now in circulation, restored to 125 minutes (UCLA; Universal 1993; Kino Lorber Blu-ray 2020), reinstates the erotic 'Dance of the Naked Moon' performed to seduce the Christian heroine, Poppaea's milk bath with partial nudity, and arena sequences of naked women set upon by beasts, the material cut for the 1938 reissue under the Code. Impurity staged as spectacle around the martyrs is not something a reader can weigh with a warning. A cut reissue (1938, or the 1944 version with a war prologue) could be reconsidered only if a copy is identifiable and the Legion's classification of it is found.
summary: DeMille's pre-Code epic of Christians martyred under Nero, notorious for the orgy and arena scenes that helped bring about the Legion of Decency.

summary: Ida Lupino's convent-school comedy follows Hayley Mills as a prank-playing pupil whose long war with Rosalind Russell's Mother Superior ends in a vocation.
synopsis: Mary Clancy arrives at St Francis Academy, a girls' school run by nuns, and at once teams up with Rachel Devery. Over three years the pair stage a string of pranks that test the patience of the Mother Superior, who comes close to sending Mary away; Mary's uncle, her guardian, lets her stay on. When Mother Superior learns what lies behind Mary's behaviour, she shows mercy and sees promise in her. Left at school over Christmas, Mary watches the sisters at Midnight Mass from the wings of the chapel. When old Sister Liguori dies in her sleep, Mary slips into the chapel and sees Mother Superior's private grief. At graduation Mary announces that she will stay and enter the order. Rachel feels betrayed, but comes to accept her friend's choice.
inclusion: This is a mild studio comedy, but an unusually honest one about a vocation. It comes from Jane Trahey's memoir of a Catholic girls' school in the 1930s, and the sisters are individuals rather than saints or tyrants: Simcha Fisher notes that several carry painful pasts and share real friendships. Rosalind Russell, a devout Catholic, gives Mother Superior dry wit and authority, and her grief at a sister's death is the best scene in the film. Hayley Mills is better than her material. The weaknesses are real. Variety found the plotting repetitive, most contemporary critics thought it formulaic, the slapstick has dated, and Fisher would cut twenty minutes. The turn from farce to vocation is abrupt; Christian Sauvé finds the late revelation forced. It was Lupino's last feature, and it remains a good family film that treats the convent as a real way of life.
themes: Religious life is shown as it was before the Council: full habits, community prayer, Midnight Mass and obedience to a superior. The film takes the vocation seriously without preaching. Mary is not converted by argument. She is drawn by seeing the sisters at prayer at Christmas and by the quiet way the community meets a death, and her choice is presented as a free answer, not an escape. Mother Superior's authority rests on charity: she disciplines, then forgives. There are no doctrinal statements to weigh. The Catholic content is the witness of a community living its rule, seen through the eyes of a girl who begins by mocking it.
history: Jane Trahey published Life with Mother Superior in 1962, drawing on her own schooldays at a Catholic girls' school near Chicago in the 1930s; she was a day pupil, while the book's school is a boarding school. Filming began in August 1965 under the title Mother Superior, with exteriors at a Pennsylvania mansion and interiors at Columbia's Hollywood studio. A sequel, Where Angels Go, Trouble Follows, followed in 1968 without Mills.
advisories:
Slapstick pranks and mild mischief.

The death of an elderly nun, handled gently.

Simcha Fisher notes a few gags in which the camera lingers on schoolgirls' legs and bottoms for laughs.

Suitable for families; older children will enjoy it most.

title: Vision
originalTitle: Vision – Aus dem Leben der Hildegard von Bingen
alternateTitles: Vision: From the Life of Hildegard von Bingen
decision: GREY: Rule (a) does not apply. Hildegard was never formally canonised in the Middle Ages, but she was venerated as a saint and her name stands in the Roman Martyrology, as the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) records; Benedict XVI's 2012 extension of her cult adds nothing needed here. Identity (filmportal.de) and content (Christianity Today, Time Out, One Guy's Opinion, Wikipedia) are established. Reservations: von Trotta's feminist framing, ambiguity over whether Hildegard feigns illness, little sense of the mystical, and an intense, possessive attachment to Richardis.
summary: Margarethe von Trotta's handsome, measured life of St Hildegard of Bingen, with Barbara Sukowa as the visionary abbess who founds her own convent against male resistance.
synopsis: Hildegard is given as a child to the Benedictine house at Disibodenberg, where she grows up among the nuns enclosed beside the monks' abbey. As a nun she has visions, which she keeps hidden until the monk Volmar encourages her to write them down. Elected to lead the sisters, she clashes with Abbot Kuno over penitential severity, the study of medicine and the sisters' welfare, and her visions are examined and in the end accepted by Church authority. Deeply attached to the young nun Richardis, she resolves to found her own convent at Rupertsberg near Bingen, against the monks' opposition. A nun's pregnancy and suicide shake the community. When Richardis's family secures her an abbacy elsewhere, Hildegard fights bitterly to keep her and is devastated by her departure. At the end Hildegard announces that she will go out and preach.
inclusion: Hildegard was a composer, a writer on medicine and nature, a correspondent of popes and emperors and a reformer of her own community, and von Trotta's film gives a solid outline of that life. It was shot in surviving medieval monasteries, including Maulbronn and Eberbach, and Kenneth Morefield in Christianity Today credits it with careful research and much detail of convent life. Barbara Sukowa's Hildegard is formidable, even haughty, and her chant runs through the film. It is slow and severe. Joshua Rothkopf in Time Out finds the performance over-restrained and the abbess's famous independence in short supply, and a reviewer at One Guy's Opinion warns that the pacing is very deliberate. It is most alive in the Richardis story, which von Trotta called its emotional climax. Its value is as an introduction to a great medieval figure rather than as a portrait of a mystic.
themes: The visions are treated as real events, and they are tested and approved by the Church, but Morefield, citing the medievalist Elizabeth Rambo, finds little sense of the transcendent; the Hildegard on screen can look more like a shrewd politician than a mystic. Von Trotta frames the story around a woman resisting male superiors, and the film leaves open whether some of Hildegard's illnesses are feigned to get her way. The Benedictine life itself, with its Office, enclosure and obedience, is shown with respect, and questions of penance and learning are raised, though not resolved. Hildegard's possessive love for Richardis is presented as an intense friendship; Rothkopf hints at an unspoken subtext, while One Guy's Opinion finds nothing improper.
history: Hildegard (1098–1179) entered religious life as a child at Disibodenberg and in about 1147–48 settled with eighteen sisters at Rupertsberg near Bingen, where she died. The Catholic Encyclopedia records that no formal canonisation ever took place, though Gregory IX and Innocent IV ordered inquiries; she was venerated as a saint, her name is in the Roman Martyrology and her feast is 17 September. Benedict XVI extended her cult to the whole Church in 2012.
liberties: The film compresses decades into a few conflicts, concentrated on Abbot Kuno and on Richardis. Morefield notes that it raises disputes over penance and secular learning and then drops them. The nun's pregnancy and suicide and Hildegard's possible feigned illness are dramatic conjecture rather than documented fact.
advisories:
Two scenes of self-flagellation, and nuns removing a belt of thorns from a dead sister's scarred body.

A nun becomes pregnant and later takes her own life; no sexual activity is shown.

Rated 12 in Germany; suitable for teenagers and adults.

The film reads Hildegard partly through a modern feminist lens.

grey.question: Vision gives a careful, well-researched outline of St Hildegard's life and treats Benedictine life with respect. The question is the angle. Von Trotta frames the abbess as a proto-feminist resisting male superiors, lets the film wonder whether some of her illnesses were feigned to get her way, and conveys little of the mystical depth of her visions. Her attachment to Richardis is shown as intense and possessive, and some critics read more into it. Viewers can judge whether this is a fair portrait or a modern projection.
